A 5% free float at $2trn is consistent with $100bn equity raise. This would eclipse SPCX’s $83bn (including greenshoe), and dwarf the previous largest-ever IPO, ARAMCO at about $30bn. ▪ An October window: Prediction markets place the cumulative probability of an October listing at >80%, with the first two weeks of the month most likely. This window sits ahead of mega-cap earnings (late October) and US midterm elections (early November). IPO timing is uncertain and could slip to 2027. Our base case remains an October listing. ▪ Market implications: We stop short of suggesting the Anthropic IPO is outright bearish for equities. However, a supply of this magnitude could act as a headwind, dampening the right tail for mega-caps and increasing the risk of a larger, more volatile sell-off. Morgan Cross Asset Systematic Strategy Spillover momentum In this subsection, we revisit the topic of spillover momentum in QIS Risk Premia. Specifically, we use logistic regression with L1 regularization into the model to predict the direction of each strategy’s one-month-ahead return, using trend signals from both public markets and QIS strategies as predictors. The model is retrained on a rolling basis, recalibrating at the end of each month using daily observations from the previous max{2 × Lookback, 252 days}, with the final one- month period reserved as the test set. Spillover signals are calculated as twice the average predicted probability from the test set minus 0.5, i.e., 2 × (avg predicted prob − 0.5). We begin by comparing spillover momentum to the standard delta-of-a-straddle trend signal on a strategy by strategy level. At each month-end, we re-estimate both momentum signals (standard trend and spillover). If the signal is positive, we take a long position; otherwise, we exit the position. On 14 August, President Prabowo Subianto announced a 2027 budget deficit target of 2.40% of GDP – a notable tightening from the estimated 2.85% for 2026 and well within the statutory 3.00% ceiling. The administration’s commitment to a ‘balanced budget’, supported by enhanced tax collection and disciplined expenditure management (despite flagship social programs), is providing a much-needed boost to market sentiment. While the realization of tax revenues remains a key metric to watch in 2027, we consider the current fiscal direction positive. Market positioning remains highly attractive for an upside move, in our view. Both offshore and onshore investors are currently underweight duration. Onshore investors, having missed the recent IndoGB rally, are likely poised to buy on any yield upticks. Offshores, seeking alternatives as sentiment on Indian bonds cools, are likely to pivot toward Indonesia. We consider that this combination of light positioning and improving fundamentals creates a favorable environment for IndoGBs to outperform. Trade idea: Long IndoGB 5y (INDOGB 7 ¼ 05/15/32) at 6.80%. At the component level, the increase is likely to be driven entirely by a pick-up in energy inflation (+3.4pp to 13.2% y/y), reflecting the recent rise in oil prices. By contrast, food inflation is expected to ease by 0.1pp to 1.5% y/y, while core inflation should remain unchanged at 2.6% y/y. Within core inflation, we expect both goods and services inflation to remain stable at 0.9% y/y and 3.4% y/y, respectively. We still think the bigger news in determining that meeting’s outcome will be the August employment and CPI reports. In terms of the detail, the July core PCE measure rose 0.25%m/m (3.3%oya), in line with expectations, and still a firm number . The market-based core, which FOMC members have sometimes preferred to look at, was more subdued at 0.15%m/m and just 2.3% over the last three months, though the over-year-ago rate sits at 3.0%, not far off from regular core inflation. Real consumer spending was flat, held back by a drop in auto sales and a shift in the timing of annual sale events. Income growth was stronger than expected, rising 0.4% m/m, but still hasn’t kept up with inflation over the last year. The flip side of soft compensation growth is that 2Q corporate profits were very strong, and profits as a share of national income hit a new record (Profit / income ratio hits new record (PCE, GDP), Abiel Reinhart, 8/26/26). Meanwhile, the Conference Board consumer confidence index edged down in August (from 90.2 to 89.4), but the present situation index rose nearly 7 points as households reported a better view of job conditions .

The signal from jobless claims remains positive, signaling both stable job growth and downward pressure on unemployment. Following the data flow this week, we raised our 3Q GDP tracking from 2.5% to 2.75% (see US: Raising 3Q GDP to 2.75% despite wider trade deficit, Abiel Reinhart, 8/27/26). Economics Europe Blog Date 27 August 2026 Flash August HICP preview Flash inflation releases for August begin on Friday (28 Aug) with France and Spain reporting first. Germany follows on Monday (31 Aug), before Italy and the euro area aggregate on Tuesday (1 Sep). We expect headline HICP to rise to 3.44% YoY in August (2.94% prev.), its highest rate in almost three years. Our forecast is broadly in line with current market pricing. Energy will account for most of the projected rise, but services and core goods are also expected to strengthen. Core HICP is forecast to increase to 2.58% (2.48% prev.). With headline inflation likely to remain around 3.5% through year -end and broader pass-through from the energy shock still limited, we continue to expect a final 25bps ECB hike in September to 2.50%. A move beyond that would require clearer evidence of indirect or second-round effects. In fact, Warsh seemed keen to dispel any credibility concerns that have emerged over the summer. Our view is that he attempted to reclaim the narrative, which had veered away from calibrating policy in a manner that allowed the Fed to reach its dual mandate, and instead sought to reinforce that the strident march towards 2% is the principal task facing the FOMC. Clear is kind, unclear is unkind: Warsh took the opportunity to again express his disdain for forward guidance. Ironically, at almost 3,500 words, his prepared text was longer than any remarks presented by Powell and was closer to Yellen’s Jackson Hole style. Since there is no Q&A during J ackson Hole, we take his prepared remarks at face value. Said another way, the lack of questions provided Warsh with an opportunity to provide a message that could not be diluted by other commentary. He chose to use that opportunity to reiterate the priority is inflation, leaving little room for ambiguity even without forward guidance. He essentially made a case for the Fed to take action in the near term in an economy that continues to show accommodative financial conditions amongst strong growth and stable employment. A pick-up in infrastructure spending is now also gradually materializing. Clients have been asking if the outcome of the elections could jeopardize the outlook for the fiscal expansion, but we think that would require a breakdown of the government as described in the scenario above. The normalisation of monetary policy from the post-GFC regime also plays a key role in keeping bund yields higher-for-longer. We asked households how the Burnham government should go about improving the public finances. Across our entire sample , only 14% favoured tax rises. 26% of respondents saw spending cuts as the more optimal solution to improve the public finances . 15% saw “neither” tax rises nor spending cuts as an optimal solution. And 10% didn’t have a view. Support for higher taxes was concentrated among the young – but only barely at +15%. In fact, more young people thought spending cuts would be better. Where was support for spending cuts the highest? Among the older -aged population (55+), whilst those on higher incomes (> GBP 50k) also reported strong support for public spending reform (28%). Households overwhelmingly favoured corporation tax rises (32%) as the main form of tax revenue raiser at the coming budget. records.text: M Idea 12 Our Model Inputs: What's Changed We first introduced our data-driven sector model in our Time Warp initiation piece in early 2024. The model aggregates bottom-up inputs across: 1) fundamental factors that we have identified to have sustainably high Sharpe ratios over decades, 2) thematics such as AI, M&A, and various policy exposures, and 3) macro rotations that we anticipate at the current stage of the cycle. We also remind readers that while our model includes various quantitative inputs, our approach is different to a standard quant - our selection of the thematic and cycle components of our model is entirely subjective and we regularly change the model weights of our quant factors based on latest performance trends, anticipated Sharpes, and our cycle expectations. We also extensively quality check the stock-level data together with our sector analysts making manual adjustments where relevant e.g. adjusting accruals data for M&A, factoring in latest headcount change announcements into employee change, adjusting management sentiment score changes if members of management presenting earnings change QoQ, etc. Our country model and combined stock screens use the same inputs as our sector model, so simply represent a different way of presenting the same underlying stock-level data. A sustained acceleration in wage inflation would likely require a clearer improvement in payroll growth and a continued stabilization in labor market conditions. While the recent ADP data suggest some tentative improvement, it is too early to conclude that a durable trend has emerged. Crucially, we do not expect a material uptick in next week's payrolls report, forecasting 40k and 50k for private and total respectively (consensus: 50k and 58k). As such, the principal challenge to the upside wage-inflation narrative remains a continuation of the recent “jobless expansion” dynamic, in which output growth accrues disproportionately to capital rather than labor. That said, with the savings rate remaining near historically low levels, our economists view such a dynamic as increasingly difficult to sustain over the medium term. Micro-level studies find that outlays on renovations tend to be front-loaded in the years immediately following a purchase and taper off as owners settle in. But with fewer home sales (again, Figure 1) and less mobility than in the past, the weak housing market is now depressing spending on the durable goods (e.g., building materials, fixtures, applianc- es) that constitute residential investment in improvements. Despite the economic health of upper-income households, who tend to be more likely to own their own homes and who have accounted for a disproportionate share of improvement spending in recent years (Figure 3), owners deterred from relocating by high financing costs have not chosen to reno- vate their existing homes instead. records.text: M Idea 8 The effective tariff rate, tariff receipts, and refunds Tariffs averaged 6.8% over April-June, and we expect that it will rise to near 10% USTR's final forced-labor Section 301 action was broadly in line with our expectations. Effective July 24, the agency imposed additional tariffs on imports from 60 economies, setting a 10% duty on economies that have adopted, partially adopted, or committed to adopt a forced-labor import prohibition and a 12.5% duty on most others. The final action also preserves several key carve-outs, including goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs, USMCA-compliant imports, and a range of general and country-specific product exemptions. Overall, both the tariff structure and the principal exemptions closely resemble the proposal, reinforcing our expectation that Section 301 would serve as the broad country-level tariff floor. We continue to expect that the statutory effective tariff rate will converge toward ~10% by year-end. In the June 2026 data, the effective tariff rate is estimated at ~6.8%. Over the past three months of detailed trade data (April, May and June), the tariff rate has averaged 6.8%. There has been a recent escalation of trade disputes with Canada, and section 338 tariffs have been applied on approximately $20bn of Canadian imports. LLC Oil Comment: How Much Oil Is the Gulf Exporting? 27 August 2026 | 7:32PM EDT Measuring oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf is n getting harder. More tankers are leaving the Gulf with their AIS/transponders switched off (“dark crossings”), satellite coverage remains limited, and ship-to-ship transfers are picking up. As a result, reported Gulf export estimates are being revised higher, with upward revisions trending higher since June to around 4mb/d currently1 (Exhibit 1). Using two independent methods, we estimate recent total Gulf exports at roughly 15-16mb/d (Exhibit 2)—still 7-8mb/d below pre-war levels, but 5-6mb/d above the March trough (Exhibit 3). Our first method puts recent Gulf oil exports at about 15mb/d. It combines Kpler n latest reported estimates with vintages of past estimates to adjust for a familiar pattern: exports are often revised higher in later weeks as “dark crossing” tankers switch signals back on farther from the Gulf.2 These upgrades are broad-based across countries and concentrated mostly in crude oil (Exhibit 4). records.text: tic supply chain Tin is increasingly attracting the attention of policymakers as governments seek to strengthen critical mineral supply chains. This reflects concerns over the concentration of global tin mining and processing in a limited number of countries, as well as the metal’s importance in semiconductors, electronics, defence systems and AI-related infrastructure. Against this backdrop, the US has become increasingly proactive. Despite being the world’s second-largest tin consumer, the country remains heavily reliant on imports, with approximately 75% of domestic tin requirements sourced from overseas. To this point, the US policy is increasingly targeting both domestic capacity and overseas resource security. On this topic, we highlight some of the recent developments: • On the upstream side, the most notable development is the announcement last month from Noronex, an Australian-listed exploration company, of the acquisition of the Sleitat Tin Project in Alaska, one of the very few significant undeveloped tin deposits in the US. Although these projects are unlikely to contribute materially to supply in the near term, they represent one of the few opportunities to establish a domestic source of primary tin concentrate and reduce long-term import dependence. • Further downstream, in September 2024, the Department of Defense awarded US$19 million to Nathan Trotter to establish comprehensive domestic tin smelting, refining and recycling capacity. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 15 Fiscal variables do not map stably to long rates In the end, investors, not models, judge debt sustainability. Academic approaches use models with variables such as real interest rates (r) and economic growth (g), while investors must judge for themselves the acceptable yield to take on sustainability risks. Research that addresses debt sustainability usually leaves open the question of how investors judge sustainability themselves and how prices differ for sustainable versus unsustainable debt loads. Markets price many risks concurrently, which makes judging the proportion of a government bond yield related to debt sustainability concerns challenging, and the component of a yield thought to house sustainability concerns, the term premium, houses many other investor concerns as well. Academic research has tried to link debt and deficits to movements in government bond yields. Researchers at the International Monetary Fund, Furceri et al (2025), replicated the approach used by Laubach (2009) and previously Laubach (2003), and their conclusions mirrored those of Laubach: the link between long-term rates and fiscal variables does not remain stable over time. • The inconsistency in Laubach's results likely comes from the context in which markets incorporate expectations for supply and how central banks respond. records.text: we are confident that the next Riksbank move will be a hike - but the timing is uncertain. What argues for the Riksbank to wait until 2027 is that this would grant time to gain confidence in the growth and labour market turnaround. Both have repeatedly disappointed, and policy normalisation without the recovery sustainably on track carries risk, which a majority on the board appears unwilling to take at the moment. However, we also acknowledge ongoing Middle East tensions have increased the risks for an earlier hike. The longer the conflict persists, the higher the risk of larger supply chain disruptions and inflationary pressures, and the higher the risk of monetary policy tightening abroad, which could lead to SEK depreciation. We therefore have recently changed our call and now consider December 2026 as the most likely date for lift-off. A hike in September, as priced with a 35% probability by markets, appears too early to us, given that this would require a surprise change in the Riksbank's communication that in our view is not warranted at this stage. After December, we expect the Riksbank to pause in March and May but hike a second time to 2.25% in June 2027, bringing policy to a neutral stance in a slow and gradual manner. BOND WATCH Real money remains cautious on EM debt Figure 6 EM debt flows Headwinds to EM local currency debt are plentiful: attractive real yields, favorable inflation dynamics, a softer USD and enhanced policy credibility. That said, investor participation remains selective rather than indiscriminate. Real money buying across EM regions remains weak with a near -50th percentile flow pattern in EM Europe but various gradations of selling elsewhere (Figure 6). Two things to note. First, this in part reflects a continued rotation into EM equities – 20- day flows into aggregate EM equities reside in the top decile. Second, EM FI flow patterns are generally weaker following the latest rise in oil prices related to the Middle East, evidence once again that the real money investor base remains sensitive to geopolitical shocks and commodity price volatility given its outsized impact on food and fuel prices, which are large constituents of EM inflation baskets. We might be seeing the lagged transmission of the earlier ECB rate cuts. Private sector balance sheets are healthy, which would aid transmission. Maybe structural demand from AI investment and defence spending is offsetting higher energy costs and geopolitical uncertainty. In short, maybe what Europe is facing is a positive demand story, not just a negative supply story. Having quickly dropped to 48.8 in April, the composite PMI rose to 52.1 in August and might have been higher were it not for heat -related headwinds in services. That said, there are reasons to be cautious about growth. The energy shock is not over. Gas prices have reached a new high for the year, raising the prospect of an electricity -based production cost shock to add to the existing oil-based transport cost shock. Note that the 2Q profit improvement is not related to IEEPA refunds, which don’t affect NIPA profits. Lower post-IEEPA tariffs also played only a small role in the 2Q profit increase: annualized profits rose $400bn q/q whereas customs duties ex IEEPA refunds—which subtract from pre-tax profits—only fell $20bn. One possible source of slippage between profits and hiring could be the industry makeup of rapid profit growth. The industry breakdown for 2Q is not yet available, so we illus- trate by looking at net income for S&P 500 firms (Table 1). Over half of profit growth in the last year has come just in technology. That industry has been steadily losing employ- ment since late 2022 and is well below the pre-COVID trend, despite consistently high earnings. And while we aren’t over- ly worried about an AI-induced job apocalypse, some of the profit growth here is arguably premised on the idea of saving labor in other sectors. records.text: Ronnie Walker +1(917)343-4543 | ronnie.walker@gs.com Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC US Daily: Friday’s Preliminary Benchmark Revision to Payrolls: No Longer Negative 27 August 2026 | 8:54AM EDT On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) will publish a preliminary estimate n of the benchmark revision to March 2026 nonfarm payrolls. Based on the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW)—the key source data for the annual benchmark revision—an upward revision seems likely; we estimate on the order of 50-450k (or a 5-40k upward revision to monthly payroll growth over April 2025-March 2026). If realized, this would be the first upward benchmark revision since 2022. n Difficulties accounting for unauthorized workers likely caused the QCEW to understate job growth and contributed to the deeply negative benchmark revisions of the last three years. The undercounting of unauthorized workers is less of an issue for this year’s benchmark because immigration has slowed sharply over the last two years. The preliminary benchmark revision has underestimated the final revision in each n of the last six years, by roughly 100k on average. This reflects that the QCEW itself has been revised up in every quarter since 2019 with the exception of 2020H1. Revisions to the QCEW are one reason why the BLS only benchmarks payrolls to the QCEW annually and with a long lag. records.text: eport. Key Takeaways Nonfinancial corporate profits rose by an outsized $400.9bn in 2Q 26, pushing profit margins near post-WW2 highs. In our view, the most important driver is pricing power: firms raised per unit prices substantially in the quarter while labor and nonlabor costs were flat. This behavior has been going on since "Liberation Day"; firms have offset higher tariff-related costs by restraining labor costs and raising prices. The dynamic resembles corporate behavior COVID: strong pricing power supported margins while squeezing household purchasing power. The 2Q profit surge is unlikely to persist. High prices erode purchasing power. We expect profit growth to normalize as inflation recedes and labor costs firm. The FY2026 budget assumes an interest rate of 3.0%, which is already functioning as a fiscal threshold for the average 10y yield. Our projected rates path places the FY2026 average at approximately 2.87%, only modestly below that threshold. Our estimates indicate that a 100bp increase in rates adds merely around JPY0.6tn to annual interest expenditure in the first year, implying a gradual near-term cash-flow effect. Nevertheless, the process through which the assumed rate is progressively raised to reflect prevailing market levels will place persistent upward pressure on the budget-request total. Importantly, a larger fiscal deficit does not translate proportionately into greater super-long issuance. The MoF reduced super-long issuance in the June 2025 revision to its plan and implemented a further reduction in the FY2026 plan. Calendar-based market issuance was lowered by JPY3.8tn to JPY168.5tn, while retail JGB issuance was increased to JPY5.9tn. For two consecutive years, the authorities have avoided concentrating supply in maturities characterised by comparatively weak demand. Recent supplementary funding has similarly relied primarily upon drawdowns of front-loaded refunding bonds and increased short- and medium-term issuance, without raising calendar-based super-long supply. Whether a series reports par value or market value matters as well. Treasury holdings data are mostly reported at market value, while primary dealer transaction data that we reference below are reported at par value. The size of the debt distracts from what matters most about it: • The speed at which the debt accumulates, i.e., the size and timing of fiscal deficits, • The risk characteristics of the debt that investors will buy, • The price at which investors will buy and the value it provides at that price, and • The major drivers of the yields in the marketplace for it.

In Profiting from Positioning Dynamics in Commodity Futures, we built a “Variation in Hedging Pressure” factor capturing the positioning dynamics of hedgers and speculators, and later designed a standardized indicator tracking the spread between short- and long-term averages of hedging pressure, extending it across equities and bonds. While this baseline positioning strategy delivers attractive stand-alone performance, two extensions warrant investigation: first, raw signals can fire prematurely since crowded positions may persist before reversing—prompting a momentum overlay as a confirmation filter in Combining Positioning Dynamics and Price Momentum in Cross Asset Futures and Tactical Trifecta; and second, contract selection along the futures curve has historically defaulted to the front contract, despite positioning, carry, and crowding varying meaningfully across the 1st through 4th generic contracts. In this study, we use our crowding metric FOMO to refine where along the futures curve to express the positioning view. records.text: upply. The question seems understandable, given the amount of bonds that investors need to purchase. Given our goal of helping investors add alpha to their portfolio, we do not see value in estimating who will buy these bonds because it would not help us predict the direction of bond prices/yields. Even if we could provide an accurate account of which investors would buy, we would also have to forecast when those investors would buy and at what price. Knowing who will buy the supply has little meaning in the absence of knowing the timing and price at which those purchases occur. What determines timing and price at which investors make the decision whether to buy, hold, or sell? More often than not, the answer comes back to the macro environment and its impact on central bank decision making. In the absence of knowing who will buy, when, and at what price, how should investors think about supply and its impact on price? We discuss the impact of supply on price in Between a Rock and a Hard Place. In short, sovereign supply moves market prices the most when expectations about it form or change from previously held expectations.

We continue to think that a mix of investment in data centres, the German fiscal package and the continued disbursements of EU funds should provide support to European capex. We also see credit growth, a leading indicator, moving up across all sectors. Nonetheless, with the downward trend in German investment continuing, data so far suggest that the capex boom is not yet there in Europe - and ultimately it is today's capex that drives future growth. The one large positive surprise of 2Q26 were exports, which have been very solid in all countries (Germany: 2.0%Q, France: 2.6%Q, Spain: 0.8%Q, Netherland: 1.2%Q). More granular data tend to be noisy, but we see two potential dynamics at play here. One is likely temporary: there is a significant push of exports of chemical products towards Asia, and it looks like the European industry benefitted from supply disruptions in the Middle East (see anecdotal evidence here for instance). With natural gas prices moving higher in Europe, this might revert. The second dynamic is likely more structural, with positive developments in European exports of machinery or electronic equipment for instance, including towards the US. Our guess would be that exports will remain a positive factor for EA growth going forward, as a stronger global economy feeds into euro area growth through this channel. We have pointed out for some time that industry in Germany is increasingly focusing on the manufacture of higher value-added products as well as product- related services. This has come at the expense of labor - and energy -intensive products, which also include many intermediate goods. The short form of this trend is: value over volume. The loss of industrial jobs in recent years is a result of this structural change, which was further exacerbated by the general period of economic weakness as well as trade and geopolitical headwinds (US tariffs, China shock). In statistics, this is reflected in the diverging trends of real gross value added (excluding intermediate goods) and the production index (including intermediate goods) in the manufacturing sector. The gap between the two time series began to open about ten years ago. It widened further in the wake of the Covid -19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine. Although Treasury futures are conventionally treated as linear rates products, USZ6 will likely become longer duration in a selloff as the CTD shifts toward lower coupon, longer duration bonds. This rising duration as rates rise creates a positively convex payoff profile. Economically, this resembles an embedded payer option, but we believe the market significantly underprices this convex payout in a selloff. We see two ways to capture the discount: long USZ6 puts and long USZ6 net basis. Schmid said that he views monetary policy as not restrictive and possibly accommodative, and aligned himself with the regional Fed presidents who dissented at the July FOMC meeting. Hammack reiterated her view that it would be appropriate for the FOMC to add monetary policy restraint, warning that keeping inflation above target for too long risks entrenching inflation expectations and making it harder to return inflation to the Fed's target. Tomorrow morning, Chairman Warsh will deliver his inaugural speech at Jackson Hole. His tendency to eschew any form of forward guidance suggests we probably won't get guidance on where the federal funds rate is headed, but task force plans, productivity and AI, and the broad sweep of history and economic philosophy could feature. They become the main market driver at certain times, but they also disappear again without the underlying issues been solved. Reason #4: The Fed needs a ‘credibility hike’ Does the US need a ‘credibility hike’? We think not. We get questions about the idea that Fed Chair Warsh needs to hike in order to stabilize the UST backend. We disagree with the idea that a more hawkish Fed can cause the curve to sustainably twist flatten. Overall twist flattening regimes are quite rare. Figure 13 below shows UST 30s vs 2s monthly changes, conditional on oil regime (previous month increase or decrease). In general, the relationship is obviously positive, but even more so when oil is also moving higher (reflecting either positive growth or a supply shock). Japan can also offer an insight on what a credibility hike could look like in terms of market reaction. For more than a year now, the JPY curve has bear steepened on the idea that the BoJ is behind the curve. After the US-Japan FX joint intervention, the market has priced a more hawkish BoJ. As shown in Figure 14, while the curve has flattened since, the backend has continued to sell off. Hence, we don’t believe a hawkish Fed will lead to backend rally. In fact, we find it hard to believe UST demand would pick up in a hawkish Fed regime. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: 2 Liquid Insight | 27 August 2026 G3 FX: Safety in numbers Markets are increasingly pricing a world of persistent fiscal pressures and elevated sovereign term premia, but not necessarily unique US fiscal challenges. Gold and global long-dated sovereign yields are near the top of 10-year ranges (Exhibit 3). While major markets may be taking their signal from US bonds, credibility gaps in Europe are exacerbating these moves. For example, France's bond market has shown a higher sensitivity to US term premia than German Bunds in the long end during the sell-off over the past few months (see Liquid Insight 26 August 2026 ). Trip hazards in the Fall Near-term risks in Japan (a budget process running through Nov/ Dec), France (difficulty finalising a 2027 budget, a potential credit downgrade in Oct and elections next year) and UK (autumn budget due Oct) could keep DXY supported even if the global debasement trade (short 30y bonds, long gold) continues to perform. DXY has largely tracked 10s30s rate differentials, which steepen as investors demand greater compensation to hold long-dated government debt (Exhibit 2). records.text: 27 August 2026 Japan Rates Strategy Page 4 Deutsche Securities Inc. these points set out a clear case for pre-emptive tightening even if headline CPI temporarily falls below 2%. His observation that the policy direction signalled at the March Wakayama press conference was implemented in June suggests that soft near-term CPI would not preclude action in September or October. He also highlighted several upside inflation factors: AI-related export prices, up 10% year on year, substantially offsetting the drag from oil-led import prices, up 17%; a return to inflation above 2% in the second half of the fiscal year; and a view that downstream pass-through has yet to run its course. The closing reference to Eiichi Shibusawa and inflation during the Satsuma Rebellion directly invoked the history of monetary financing. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 The CBO argues that high and rising debt could increase the likelihood of a fiscal crisis because investors might lose confidence in the US government's ability to service and repay its debt. The CBO also argues that it could lead to higher inflation expectations, erode confidence in the US dollar as a reserve currency, and constrain policymakers from using deficits in a countercyclical way. We liken these concerns – which the media only seem highlight when 10y yields near periodic highs – to an adult not being able to get over the common childhood fear of a bogeyman hiding under the bed, even though the bogeyman hasn't appeared, ever. Also, international benchmark crude oil prices turned up in early July and remain on an upward trend. Combined with JPY depreciation, this means import-driven inflationary pressure is likely to persist through the summer. As a result, we expect the wave of cost pass-through originating from higher crude oil prices to continue spreading to downstream products, including final consumer goods. Rice prices, by contrast, are likely to exert downward pressure. A leading indicator for new-crop rice prices is down about 40% y/y, and our analysis suggests that rice could reduce core-core CPI by around 0.3pp from October onward (see Rice prices set to fall sharply from autumn, weighing on CPI, 26 August). The pass-through from wage growth to inflation also appears to be losing momentum. records.text: Geopolitical tailwinds amplified structural refining tightness. Rising strikes n on refineries in the Middle East and Russia have further constrained already-stretched global refining capacity, pushing refined products margins to new highs. Diesel remains at the epicenter of the rally, accounting for over 40% of the $40/bbl increase in average global refined product wholesale prices since February. With unclear prospects for deescalation in the Middle East and especially Russia, and as refined products stocks continue to draw, we upgrade our diesel and gasoline margins forecast and now expect US/EU diesel margins vs. Brent to average $63/49/bbl in 2027 (vs. $27/19 in February forecast). Runs and exports plummeted amid refinery outages. A much larger percent n increase in refined product margins than in crude prices reflects the sharper decline in product supply vs. crude. Global exports of refined products declined 6mb/d (25%) year-over-year (yoy), with the Persian Gulf and Russia accounting for 75% of the decline. High refinery outages weigh on runs. Global refinery outages are still o 60% above seasonal norms, which together with disrupted crude deliveries to Asia, constrain the refining supply response to higher margins. Morgan. Bloomberg Finance L.P. The Treasury curves have been whipsawed repeatedly since the spring, and most recently in the last couple of weeks. The current flattening through the late-July base pattern breakout zones derailed the developing medium-term steepening trend momentum, and have left the curves at the lower end of the spring-summer ranges with mixed technical setups. records.text: 2 Insights Resistance is futile. When it comes to long-term debt sales, a major issue facing the US Treasury is that the US is no longer the only game in town. AI investment has led to a sharp increase in long duration corporate debt issuance, a fact bemoaned by Bessent last week when he argued they should be issuing more in the belly (3-7yr) part of the curve. Five megacap companies are expected to issue around $250bn in debt in 2026, double their $120bn in 2025. $400bn is estimated for 2027. At the same time, Japanese flows have turned much less supportive. As we wrote here, and as Figure 2 illustrates, in four of the last six years, Japan has seen a surplus is net portfolio flows into long-term debt as rising JGB yields make them attractive again both for overseas and domestic investors. In the first half of 2026 Japanese investors actually sold over $50bn in overseas long-term debt leading to a net surplus of over $110bn. That is money not going into USTs. How is your $16bn looking now Scott? Live long and prosper So what does all of this mean for FX markets? For now at least, higher yields are offering the dollar some support but, this may not be true for much longer. The 3m correlation between changes in the DXY and changes in yields is falling sharply for longer-duration yields (Figure 3). For the 30-yr it is now at just 12% and i28% for 10-yr yields. Rising yields due to strong growth and the potential for or actual short-end rate hikes are clearly a dollar positive.

PLM hedging, introduced in early 2022, with mandatory adoption by 2023, represented the greatest step forward in the accounting treatment of prepayable bank assets in years and was a step forward from the last-of-layer method that came out in 2017. Both focus on a closed portfolio of assets (rather than individual securities), but last-of-layer only allowed for a hedge up to the amount of notional expected to still be outstanding at the end of the hedge term. PLM improved on this, along with other clarifications, by allowing for other “layers” with shorter terms to more effectively hedge the larger outstanding of the securities in earlier periods. The inputs for this methodology won’t capture structural features or bugs (like rent control) but can be used to identify markets that are hitting their nadirs. Lenders and bond investors may care more about the cross-sectional analysis, though they shouldn’t ignore the self-history approach. Equity aims for upside while debt aims to preserve princi- pal and earn a coupon. Cross-sectional analysis can help identify better markets to lend to today in relation to others, but lenders should also be cognizant of whether the markets are caught in a down or updraft. Are you lending to a market that is cross-sectionally strong today but one that is worsening against its own history? Ideally, lenders should consider markets where the cross-sectional rankings are relatively strong and the self-history scores are bottoming out or improving. records.text: This would not, however, necessarily entail an increase in super-long issuance. The MoF has reduced super-long supply for two consecutive years and lowered calendar-based market issuance to JPY168.5tn. We assume a third round of reductions from April 2027, with incremental funding weighted towards short- and medium-term JGBs, retail JGBs and front-loaded refunding bonds. Fiscal supply pressure should therefore be concentrated in the front end and belly rather than the super-long sector. We would not recommend pursuing steepening positions. Of the approximately 2.9% 10y yield, around 1.8% already reflects term premium; meanwhile, life insurers have been net purchasers of super-long JGBs for two consecutive months, while foreign investors have rotated from selling the belly to purchasing super-long maturities. Fiscal expansion should instead lend further support to the BoJ’s prospective hiking path—in October 2026, January 2027 and April 2027, towards a terminal rate of 1.75%—and place pressure on the same belly sector that is likely to absorb additional supply. We therefore maintain the 5s20s flattener as our principal recommendation, at 161bp with a target of 125bp. The principal risk is a change in the fiscal regime. Only if unspecified requests were to crystallise alongside a substantial supplementary budget and ultimately result in pressure on the BoJ to undertake unrequited purchases would the flattener move into a stop-loss regime. We retain 30y payer tails as protection

Regardless, whether the government chooses to reduce overall fiscal debt, channel windfall revenues into a "reserves" fund to smooth future spending when revenue conditions weaken, or a combination of both, we believe these actions all point toward a stronger fiscal position. Beyond macro fundamentals, we see two significant flow-based catalysts for a KTB rally. ▪ Over the past year, South Korean life insurers have reduced their long-end demand because rising rates caused the net present value of their liabilities to fall faster than their assets, due to a duration mismatch. If rates start to rally, this flow should reverse, creating a strong bid for long- end KTBs – a move that can be triggered by a decline in 2027 bond issuance, in our view. ▪ KTBs have been pressured since the start of this year, with retail investors rotating out of debt to chase the South Korean equity rally. However, following the equity correction in July, we see that their equity exposure has significantly reduced. Overall, we believe this rotation has concluded, removing a major headwind for the fixed-income market. PLN: Poland maintains the loosest fiscal policy among the CE3 (4% of GDP primary deficit), ranking quite high on our fiscal vulnerability index. CHF and NOK: Switzerland and Norway record the lowest fiscal vulnerability scores within the G10, with Norway exhibiting almost no fiscal risk. Meanwhile, expectations for a BoJ rate hike increased following a report on 26 August that Governor Ueda would not attend the Jackson Hole symposium and that Board Member Tamura would attend in his place (Nikkei, 26 August), prompting a modest rise in short/medium-term yields. The market subsequently remained range-bound in the absence of fresh catalysts. We have described 50bp of hikes as good risk management: it signals the ECB’s commitment to price stability on the one hand without overly burdening economic growth in the context of a negative energy supply shock on the other. The risks are skewed towards the ECB hiking further into mildly restrictive territory. First, still elevated energy prices, in particular the renewed rise in gas prices, adds further persistence risk to the inflation outlook. Second, the resilience of growth could increase the risk of indirect and second-round effects. Put differently, there might need to be rapid resolution in the Middle East and faster normalisation of energy prices if the hike to 2.50% in September is to be the final hike. Nevertheless, given summer liquidity is typically thin, leaving the market vulnerable to exaggerated price moves, many market participants have been more tactical and relatively quick in taking profit. Act II — the debasement trade returns The second leg began as gold was taking a breather and attempting to rebase around $4,400. The trigger was the US Treasury’s announcement that it would double the size of buybacks in longer-dated bonds. The programme is modest relative to the Treasury market and was originally intended for liquidity management, but the signal was powerful: investors interpreted it as a greater willingness to lean against pressure at the long end of the curve. Fiscal credibility and debt sustainability, long-running arguments for strategic gold exposure, moved back to the centre of the debate. Whether framed as "de-dollarisation", "de-fiatisation" or "debasement", the portfolio implication is similar: gold can serve as a diversifier, a hard asset and a source of resilience across a wider range of macro outcomes. Key Takeaways In October 2022, the US public debt hit $31 trillion and we wrote "The 31 Trillion Dollar Distraction" in response to the media coverage that resulted. Since then, the US public debt has climbed to $40 trillion and the media responded with more warnings about the fiscal largesse of the federal government. In October 2022, 10y yields reached 4.35% – 40bp lower than their recent 4.75% peak – putting into perspective the concession for the additional $9 trillion. We think the CBO's 4.4% long-term projection for 10y Treasury yields overstates them by at least 100bp, if core PCE inflation returns to 2% as it projects. In what follows, we embellish our October 2022 note with additional perspective on the public debt and purposefully abstain from any fear-mongering. The minutes of the July meeting contained a wide discussion of such issues. “All” members of the Governing Council agreed to “pause” at the meeting, although “some” would not have opposed a hike. The decision to pause was not controversial as the June inflation report was softer than expected, wage signals remained quite contained, inflation expectations were still seen as anchored and the situation in the Middle East was “fragile, rather than acute”. This was certainly a stronger performance than the 0.2% q/q expected by the ECB. Based on the countries who have reported so far, the resilience of domestic demand is an encouraging signal with household consumption holding up despite the inflation shock. Conversely, the negative contribution from inventories has been surprising. Importantly, however, headline HICP was expected to be back down to the 2% target from Q3-27 and stay there through to the end of 2028. It is important to remember the baseline staff forecast in June was conditioned on policy rates rising to 2.75%. But despite sticky core inflation, it is difficult to imagine monetary policy tightening much further if headline inflation is sustainably returning to target within a year. As such, the near-term path for policy could depend critically on whether the Governing Council believes core inflation will converge down to headline in the medium term or headline converges up to core. The former is less hawkish, the latter is more hawkish. Which of these two outcomes seems more or less likely to the Governing Council will depend on how it judges the risk of inflation persistence. This is a function of pricing power, bargaining power and purchasing power. Our view is there is some risk of persistence, but not as much as 2022 and not enough to warrant an outright restrictive policy stance. Not yet, at least. Our 2.50% baseline might be too optimistic, but 3.00% feels too restrictive. 2.75% is a grey zone: a non -negligible possibility unless the situation in the Middle East is resolved quickly and energy prices normalise rapidly. The principal mechanism for downward adjustment—MoF scrutiny—was scarcely evident in the preceding round. For FY2026, requests of JPY122.4tn were reduced only marginally, to an initial budget of approximately JPY122.3tn. In light of that precedent, an expectation that the JPY135tn working assumption will be reduced materially by year-end appears difficult to sustain. The figure already exceeds the JPY133.5tn FY2025 budget after supplementary appropriations. Any contention that the fiscal stance is restrictive relative to GDP therefore depends upon the implausible assumptions that unspecified requests will be nil and that no supplementary budget will be introduced. In our assessment, JPY135tn should be regarded not as the ceiling for FY2027 expenditure, but as the floor. This constitutes the appropriate starting point for the analysis. records.text: ab 28 August 2026 Global Research Japan Macro Watch September hike on track as inflation builds Slightly dovish Himino, but September hike view holds Deputy Governor Himino's speech struck a slightly dovish tone given that markets have already priced in an 80–90% probability of a September rate hike. Unlike previous occasions, he refrained from making explicit remarks supporting further tightening, instead reiterating the Bank's standard position that policy decisions will be carefully discussed at each meeting. He also stopped short of endorsing a faster pace of rate hikes, a topic highlighted in the latest Summary of Opinions, merely noting that it would continue to be examined and discussed. Likewise, he offered no direct assessment of the sharp increase in market expectations for tightening over the past mon th. That said, while the speech provided limited direct guidance on near-term policy, it expressed stronger concern than before about upside inflation risks. Himino again emphasized the risk of falling behind the curve, warning that delayed action could ultimately require more aggressive rate hikes. Although we came away with the impression that the BoJ wants to preserve the option of an October hike, we continue to view a September rate increase as the most likely scenario. Meanwhile, Fed Chair Warsh’s Jackson Hole remarks were some- what more hawkish than the message he delivered at the July FOMC press conference. Most notably, he observed that underlying inflation trends have not meaningfully improved, and that if they don’t “we have work to do.” It was also significant that he walked back two stumbles he made at the last press conference. First, after casting doubt on the future of the Fed’s inflation target, he said today: “there should be no misunderstanding: The Fed’s price-stability objective of 2 percent, as measured by the personal consump- tion expenditures (PCE) price index, is a firm, fixed target.” Second, after equivocating on what tool the Fed should rely on to achieve its objective, today he said, “ short-term interest rates are the predominant tool to achieve the dual mandate.” Both these were welcome clarifications. Markets went from pricing about a one-in-three chance of a Sep- tember hike before these remarks to around a one-in-two chance now. CE3 is well exposed to these themes (see our CE3 FX update and mid-year outlook), with the added idiosyncratic factor of the draw- down and disbursement of EU funds. This sets the stage for trading a pro-cyclical CE3 out- look and structural growth improvement (i.e. higher rates & rates carry). We see the recent softer growth patch as noise in the trend rather than a sea change. 2Q CEE growth data came in weaker than expected and higher frequency data has recently surprised to the downside, with EASIs falling in Czechia and Hungary; Poland is an excep- tion where data is heating up. At the same time, record low Danube water levels are weighing on CEE energy production and pose growth headwinds if sustained (see here). We are inclined to look through this soft patch of data and external risks, though. Incoming EU funds are set to boost CEE capex and growth (particularly in Hungary), risks are skewed to upward GDP revisions (Czechia) and the economic impact of extreme European weather is likely manageable overall. Ongoing softness in headline inflation makes it hard to frame the immediate CEE trading environment as “reflationary”, but persistent core inflation and brewing glob- al inflation risks bias us in this direction. We see a potential ‘fiscal risk-off’ catalyst out of the US in the coming months, driven by doubts about Fed credibility. Although the Treasury doubled 10y+ buyback sizes to manage long-end yields, we view this as an inadequate defense against declining Fed credibility (see US rates: Buybacks necessary, but not sufficient, dated 19 August). Ultimately, Fed policy will be decisive. Rate hikes alone will not compress term premiums – markets need a sharp upward repricing of rate expectations to achieve stability (see US long-end rates: Darned if they hike, darned if they don’t, dated 5 August). The last two benchmark revisions in particular have been quite negative, in our view likely reflecting difficulties accounting for unauthorized workers in the QCEW. (This potential undercounting is less of an issue for this year’s benchmark given the sharp slowdown in immigration, and should also be less of an issue going forward.) As we noted a few years ago, since the QCEW is based on unemployment insurance records, it likely excludes most unauthorized workers, who contributed strongly to employment growth in the periods covered by those benchmark revisions. In most cases unauthorized workers do not qualify for unemployment insurance, so employers might see little reason to pay unemployment insurance tax on their behalf and might even see it as a needless risk in the cases of any immigrants they are employing who do not yet have work permits. The second leg was a debasement trade, catalysed by the US Treasury’s decision to double the size of long-dated bond buybacks. We retain a constructive outlook and see growing upside risk if fiscal sustainability becomes a more persistent driver of strategic allocations. A hawkish Fed remains the principal near-term risk, but we would view a tighter-policy-induced pullback as an opportunity to add exposure. Top-down: The USD-EUR terminal rate differential is not particularly tight The USD-EUR terminal rate differential (proxied by Dec-27 SOFR versus €STR) is currently around 130bp. Is that too tight? Historically, the USD-EUR r* differential has ranged from -50bp to 250bp (HLW estimates). It tends to be tight during financial crises, as the US is more prone to boom/bust cycles, or when fiscal policy is relatively more expansive in Europe, as during the GFC, the 2001 dot -com bubble and the 1990s double whammy of German reunification and the S&L crisis in the US . Conversely, the spread tends to be wide during a capex boom , usually US -driven, or when the US has comparatively more expansive fiscal policy, as during the Reagan years. The best-performing currencies in August have been at the intersection of decent carry, cyclicality and relative growth momentum (our global EASI growth momentum basket is up +7% YTD). A layer-by-layer look at bank PLM activity In this piece, we’ll go into detail on banks’ usage of the portfolio-layer method (PLM) hedg- ing and what we can (and can’t) determine from the various disclosures in quarterly filings and the call reports. Prior to PLM, banks had some limited ability to hedge prepayable assets through last-of-layer, but the introduction of PLM and the sell-off in 2022 spurred more banks to consider hedging AFS securities while receiving beneficial accounting treatment. We can see that the amount of bonds included in closed portfolios for the sake of hedging has grown, as has the notional of hedges on the other side of them. Like all things banks, there is a large dispersion in how individual institutions approach this tool in their portfolio man- agement, with just under half of the largest 50 appearing to use PLM at all. The growth in closed portfolios, as well as buying in CMO floaters, leads us to iclude that a greater share of AFS assets are closer to floating rates than they have been in the past, but the majority remain unhedged fixed . Swedish CPIF: Headline and core up to 0.9% and 0.8% y/y After the likely trough in July, when the peak impact of disinflationary fiscal measures occurred, we expect August inflation (out on 7 September) to increase. Based on electricity futures until 28 August, we expect both CPIF and CPIF ex energy to rise by 0.2pp, to 0.9% y/y and 0.8% y/y, respectively. Overall, we believe this rotation has concluded, removing a major headwind for the fixed-income market. Monetary policy and FX: The correlation between USDKRW and inflation expectations in South Korea has historically pushed rates higher. However, the recent currency move provides a buffer for the BoK. USDKRW has dropped from 1,550 to 1,380 (about an 11% appreciation), driven by persistent exporter conversions. We estimate this move is equivalent to approximately 50bp of policy tightening in terms of inflation impact. This FX strength gives the BoK room to be more measured, in our view. While the market is aggressively pricing in about 107bp of rate hikes over the next year (Figure 3), we expect a much more conservative path: one hike between August and October and one more in Q1 2027 (see South Korea & Taiwan: What are the risks around upcoming rate decisions?, dated 5 August). We still think the bigger news in determining that meeting’s outcome will be the August employment and CPI reports. In terms of the detail, the July core PCE measure rose 0.25%m/m (3.3%oya), in line with expectations, and still a firm number . The market-based core, which FOMC members have sometimes preferred to look at, was more subdued at 0.15%m/m and just 2.3% over the last three months, though the over-year-ago rate sits at 3.0%, not far off from regular core inflation. Real consumer spending was flat, held back by a drop in auto sales and a shift in the timing of annual sale events. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 28 August 2026 Citi Research 3 G20 could be a turning point The focus is on the 50-day moving average as an indicator of possible change in the positions of trend followers. Thus far yen interest rates have remained above this, and it appears short positions have been maintained as interest rates have trended upward. The pricing of BoJ rate hikes has increased particularly in the short- and medium-term sectors, and the turning point is some distance away. There have been near-term position adjustments based on the outlook for the pace of rate hikes and the terminal rate, but we do not envisage any decline in interest rates. The turning point is relatively closer for the super-long sector. The flattening of the curve is also providing support. From this perspective, it does not appear likely that there is a short bias in positions. The LCH-JSCC is recovering after a drop in June, and there has been flattening since end-July, so we think foreign investors have built new flatteners. This would suggest that if there is short covering it will be relative to a range of bear strategies. Much of this will likely be risk held by Japanese institutional investors. Trends in US interest rates are still key. records.text: 42 Dobromir Tzotchev, PhD AC (44-20) 7134-5331 dobromir.tzotchev@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 28 August 2026 J P M O R G A N Revisiting trend following in inflation swaps Inflation and the central bank policy response remain top investor concerns, especially given recent sharp commodity price moves—notably in energy, where geopolitical disruptions have reset price levels. Persistent core inflation above target in both the US and Eurozone continues to delay the anticipated easing cycle, keeping inflation risk in focus across asset classes. Inflation swaps offer direct exposure to expected inflation levels and surprises. In Protecting against inflation, we found supportive evidence for trend-following strategiesin 10Y inflation swaps, 10Y rates, and oil as protection against both upside and downside moves in realized and expected inflation, along with attractive diversification benefits. In Ideas to hedge for inflation risk we analyzed the convexity of commodity trend-following versus realized inflation. This publication extends that study by incorporating inflation swaps across a broader maturity spectrum, using indices tracking rolling zero-coupon inflation swaps with tenors of 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10 years, in both USD and EUR, to exploit diversification across the inflation curve. records.text: LLPAs would likely be lower on the cleanest credits, and base g-fees could possibly come down. That would benefit the headline primary rates, which would be an optical win. In addition, reductions in cross subsidy might mean more competitive pricing for jumbos, investor loans, second homes, etc.—parts of the footprint that are currently being siphoned away to bank portfolios and PLS thanks to better execu- tion. Depending on how it’s structured, it might be considered to be positive in expectation for the GSE earnings (though with the very low default rates we’ve seen recently, backward looking earnings have probably been boosted by just doing more total business). Relatedly, after the Treasury Secretary’s intervention at the long end of the curve, we’ve also been fielding questions about whether the administration might be back in a ‘try anything’ mindset with respect to mortgage rates. Their other plausible levers include FHA MIPs and GSE purchases as means to temporarily reduce rates. We think it’s a little late in the year (having passed the peak homebuying season) and we’re at too high a level of rates for them to do much there. FHA MIPs are already about as low as they should go to cover expected losses, with much of the health of the MMI fund resting on the actuarial strength of 2020/2021 vintages rather than current origination. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures The 2027 economic package, due on 8 September, will serve as the first true test of whether the electoral cycle will derail the fiscal path. We expect the package to fall short of the government's signaled consolidation. We forecast a 2027 public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) deficit of 4.3% of GDP – well above the official 3.5% target – with primary surpluses too thin to stabilize public debt. Rigid spending leaves a narrow base for adjustment: Pensions, social transfers and non-programmable spending account for 81.6% of total federal expenditure and are structurally poised for growth. Contributory pensions are driven by demographics, while non-contributory social programmes, which are central to the administration’s political platform, were written into the constitution in 2024. They can no longer be reduced through the annual budget process, so they sit outside the set of spending lines the Finance Ministry can actually adjust. With revenue-sharing and debt service largely formulaic, the administration is left with difficult arithmetic: the Finance Ministry’s own guidelines call for a reduction in expenditure of 1.6pp of GDP in 2027, and that adjustment has to come out of the less than one-fifth of total spending that remains genuinely discretionary, precisely when political incentives run in the opposite direction. records.text: A Full Recovery in Runs Requires Global Geopolitical Deescalation Global refinery runs did not increase even during the June ceasefire in the Middle East despite a temporary recovery in total oil flows from the Persian Gulf, suggesting that a sustainable recovery in runs requires geopolitical deescalation in both the Middle East and Russia. We upgrade our 2026Q4 US/Europe diesel margins vs. Brent by $29/34/bbl to $75/65/bbl correspondingly and upgrade US/Europe gasoline margins to $29/21/bbl. Assuming that Middle Eastern unplanned outages gradually moderate by mid-2027 and Russian refinery outages persist through next year, we see global refinery runs increasing by 2.4mb/d by year-end from August levels, but recovering to their seasonal norms only in 2027H2 as high-margin-driven runs in unconstrained regions offset Russian outages (Exhibit 7). A further increase in refinery utilization rates outside of the Middle East and Russia is challenging because higher Asian runs require better crude availability and the removal of export constraints (i.e. quota system in China), while US refineries are already running near operational limits. A light expected fall maintenance season also increases the risk of unplanned refinery outages in 2026Q4 and 2027Q1. Together they move from empirical observation to a tradable strategy, and the discussion below draws out the key findings from each. Among the key findings, CDS index volatility moves systematically with spreads, but the surface typically behaves neither like pure sticky strike nor like full local volatility, with realised skew stickiness generally around 1.3–1.5—a persistent "sticky strike plus" regime. In iTraxx Main, option skew persistently prices more spread-vol covariance than subsequently realises, with realised covariance arriving in episodic bursts while payer skew is priced more continuously. The project pipeline remains thin Taken together, developments across key producing countries highlight the increasing fragility of global tin supply. Global production is facing mounting structural pressure as major operations mature, ore grades decline and mining conditions become increasingly complex. Indeed, ore grades have fallen by almost 18% since 2006, raising costs and constraining the availability of tin concentrates. At the same time, the supply response to higher prices has remained limited. While global tin resources remain abundant, years of underinvestment in project development have left the industry struggling to convert resources into new mine supply. Looking ahead, we estimate the current project pipeline could add roughly 30-33ktpa of mine supply by 2030, although the majority of this is unlikely to arrive before 2028-29. Importantly, none of the major projects has yet reached a final investment decision (FID), suggesting execution, permitting and financing risks remain. Within Western markets, the most advanced projects include South Crofty in the UK and Oropesa in Spain, which could both come online in 2028. In Morocco, the Achmmach project has gained fresh momentum following its acquisition by China’s Xingye Silver & Tin, and could enter production as early as 2027-28. records.text: 21 Dobromir Tzotchev, PhD AC (44-20) 7134-5331 dobromir.tzotchev@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 28 August 2026 J P M O R G A N Composite Momentum - Blend the two We construct a unified Momentum Composite by blending the strongest technical and fundamental signals identified across the 37-factor study, with drawdown limitation as a central design constraint. Key Findings: The Technical Composite (12M-1M V ol Adjusted & High-to-Price) delivers a 0.71 Long/Short Sharpe at -25% max drawdown; the Fundamental Composite (Earnings Momentum 6M & Net Cashflow Revisions 3M) is the strongest single signal at 11.0% annualized and a 1.15 Sharpe. The blended Momentum Composite produces 10.8% annualized Returns, a 0.95 Sharpe, the highest Long-side Hit-Rate (62%), and the lowest Long-only Kurtosis (1.17). Blending orthogonal technical and fundamental signals delivers the cleanest, most resilient momentum exposure in the study. (Figure 22M o m e n t u m C o m p o s i t e - L / S M S C I G D M ) Taming Momentum: Beta & Vol Scaling Momentum strategies remain vulnerable to severe crash risk; we evaluate Beta- and volatility-scaling as overlays across our Momentum signals to determine which mechanism best controls drawdowns without sacrificing return. We find the portfolio implications are straightforward: vol scaling at 10% for Long/Short mandates, vol scaling at 5% for Long-only, and Beta scaling reserved for cases where market- neutrality is a hard constraint rather than a return-enhance

As a result, part of the recent widening appears to reflect a premium created by higher commodity prices rather than simply a repricing of the future commodity path itself. With oil prices around our commodity strategists' estimate of fair value, the risk of a resolution with the mid-term elections fast approaching, and a risk premium already built in, we think commodity price risk is more likely to fade than grow. The key risks to the trade is a materially stronger than expected economic data or upside to commodity prices. On the data, we believe this risk is increasingly self- limiting. Under the post-Jackson Hole reaction function, stronger activity or inflation data should generate a larger repricing of OIS expectations than earlier in the cycle. While firmer data could support inflation pricing directly, a corresponding move higher in the expected Fed path and nominal yields should offset some of that upside pressure. H o w e v e r , t h e s u r g e i n c o r p o r a t e p r o f i t s i m p l i e s u p s i d e r i s k t o w a g e i n f l a t i o n , see recoupling remains reasonable, Bruce Kasman, 08/26/26). A sustained acceleration in wage inflation would likely require a clearer improvement in payroll growth and a continued stabilization in labor market conditions. While the recent ADP data suggest some tentative improvement, it is too early to conclude that a durable trend has emerged. Crucially, we do not expect a material uptick in next week's payrolls report, forecasting 40k and 50k for private and total respectively (consensus: 50k and 58k). As such, the principal challenge to the upside wage-inflation narrative remains a continuation of the recent “jobless expansion” dynamic, in which output growth accrues disproportionately to capital rather than labor. That said, with the savings rate remaining near historically low levels, our economists view such a dynamic as increasingly difficult to sustain over the medium term. From this perspective, Bessent has delivered liquidity support, as measured by dealer balance sheets, swap spreads and spline errors , which all show improving dynamics. Term premiums, nonetheless, remain elevated (Figure 7), which is influenced by many factors outside of simple market liquidity. Fiscal sustainability is certainly encapsulated in higher premiums, as is broader inflation uncertainty. Excessive reliance on bills is also not a free lunch, as refinance risk grows with a flatter curve ; an ever-looming risk, particularly as investors and this analyst team continues to consider rate hikes a distinct possibility for the Warsh Fed. records.text: US Rates Strategy 28 August 2026 Citi Research 2 Fed Chair Warsh’s speech today at Jackson Hole was more hawkish than we expected (see US Rates Weekly - Can Secretary Bessent and Chair Warsh save the curve?). He revealed that core PCE and the unemployment rate are the two inputs to his reaction function. This is important, since UR has fallen in line with the participation rate, which is leaving little job creation. He noted the recently weaker NFP prints were a function of “labor supply barely growing” and that “labor markets are consistent with full employment”. This is a powerful statement, in our view, and explains why the front-end rally from the weaker jobs print earlier this month is now being reversed (Figure 1). He also pushed back on moderating wage growth, which has been one of our arguments for why the Fed should not hike, stating that it has “not proven a reliable indicator of future inflation for a very long time”. On inflation, he highlighted that “the Fed’s predominant focus right now should be on prices” and that “inflation is running above our 2 percent target”. He also pushed back on the recent inflation prints, stating that “while this summer's PCE and CPI readings were better than expected, they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved”. The conclusion is unambiguous: a JPY135tn budget-request total would constitute evidence of fiscal expansion, but would not, in itself, justify holding steepening positions. For protection against the fiscal tail risk, 30y payer tails offer a more efficient hedge than a carry-intensive outright short position in super-long JGBs. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 13 Daily turnover lets marginal buyers set prices Once we agree that the US government has the ability to pay back its debt, in every circumstance, then we can debate whether it has the willingness to do so. Provided we agree it has the willingness, then the money necessary to finance future deficits comes from the government's decision to increase spending or accept less tax revenue. In the end, a federal government deficit amounts to nothing more than an accounting entry on the government balance sheet – a balance sheet that differs materially from that of the corporate and household sector, given the federal government's ability to pay back its obligations. Government deficits create either public sector demand, via spending, or private sector demand, via tax cuts and financial assets, and the money the government spends, or the money that is spent and saved after a tax cut, eventually finds its way into US Treasuries. The relevant question for macro investors, however, concerns the price at which Treasury securities clear rather than the identity of the buyer. Swap spreads offer one way to examine that price. For relative value investors, like those dealing in swap spreads, the "who" matters, but macro investors should rest assured someone will buy, even if they don't know who. records.text: OMO, and the entry-timing benefit of momentum confirmation. The strategy proceeds at each weekly rebalance in three stages: 1. Asset selection (CFTC positioning): Rank the universe of 20 commodities by their HP_Score. The top 30% (most over-owned) are flagged as short candidates and the bottom 30% (most under-owned) as long candidates. 2. Contract selection (FOMO): For each flagged commodity, compute FOMO across the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th generic contracts. For long candidates pick the contract with the lowest FOMO; for short candidates pick the contract with the highest FOMO. 3. Trade confirmation (momentum): Apply the delta-of-the-straddle momentum filter to the selected contract. A long position is retained only if its momentum signal is positive; a short position is retained only if its momentum signal is negative. Candidates that fail the momentum check are dropped from the portfolio at that rebalance. The surviving names are sized using inverse-volatility weighting based on a rolling 1Y covariance matrix, and the overall portfolio is scaled to an annualized volatility target of 10%. As in the CFTC positioning + FOMO section, the trade is no longer constrained to the front-month contract –the FOMO ranking can pick any of the first four generics, though only one contract is traded per asset. records.text: Japan Macro Watch28 August 2026 ab 2 Slightly dovish Himino, but September hike view holds Deputy Governor Himino’s speech came across as somewhat dovish, given that the market has already priced in a September rate hike with an implied probability of around 80-90%. Ahead of previous rate hikes, Governor Ueda had provided more explicit guidance, stating that the Bank would “appropriately assess whether a rate hike is warranted at the next Monetary Policy Meeting.” This time, however, Deputy Governor Himino refrained from making similarly forward-looking remarks and instead reiterated the Bank’s established position that it would “carefully discuss the outlook at each policy meeting.” Regarding the pace of rate hikes, the Summary of Opinions from the July meeting included arguments that the Bank may need to accelerate the pace of tightening. However, no comparable discussion appeared in Himino’s speech. Rather, his remarks emphasized that both moving too quickly and too slowly carry risks, presenting a broadly balanced message. Against a market backdrop that has become increasingly hawkish, this could reasonably be interpreted as relatively dovish. He also avoided commenting directly on the sharp repricing of rate hike expectations that has taken place over the past month. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Financial Conditions: Easing Since the July FOMC Following the conflict in the Middle East and the uncertainty it brings to the next steps for monetary policy, we continue to track our FRB/US-based measure of financial conditions. As of the August 27 market close, financial conditions remained tighter than before the recent escalation in the Middle East, yet meaningfully easier than at the time before the July FOMC meeting. Since the July FOMC meeting, financial conditions have eased by 32bp, primarily driven by positive equity returns and U.S. dollar depreciation. The index aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. It includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate using the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since hostilities in the Middle East began on February 28, the tightening in financial conditions is equivalent to about a 22bp rise in the federal funds rate. records.text: Global FX 28 August 2026 Citi Research 2 Déjà vu 1997 After intervening in the EURJPY, in an interview with Japan’s national broadcaster NHK on August 4 Secretary Bessent cited the 1998 Asian crisis as one reason for the concerted intervention with Japan. The JPY appreciation that continued for ten years after the 1985 Plaza Accord damaged the international competitiveness of Japan’s export industries, while Asian nations very rapidly become bases for international manufacturers. On the other hand, JPY depreciation after 1995 reversed the previous optimism regarding Asian nations, and this was a distal cause of the economic crisis in South Korea, Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia. In 2005 Ben Bernanke, then a member of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, hypothesized that emerging markets had since the early 2000s accumulated more foreign currency reserves than needed as they strove to weaken their currencies and improve their international balances of payments (BoP) in preparation for another possible crisis. This theory of excessive global savings may not necessarily be correct, but it is difficult to deny that the accompanied strength of the USD was one reason for the rapid expansion in the US current account deficit at the time (Figure 1). records.text: 28 August 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 15 A sudden tightening in the €STR-DFR spread Soniya Sadeesh | Strategist | +44-20-754-73091 Note: This note was originally published on 26 August 2026 We have previously highlighted that excess liquidity is less ample than the headline level suggests. The most recent piece of evidence comes from tightening in the €STR -DFR spread. Over the past couple of weeks, the spread has moved by roughly 0.6bps. This is a sizeable compression in the context of historical daily volatility. Today’s FICOTD plots the spread against excess liquidity levels. As can be seen, the recent tightening has been larger than the recent trend would imply. While there is a risk that this reverts, it has not been accompanied by any meaningful shifts in underlying volumes nor has it occurred around key reporting dates, both of which might suggest an idiosyncratic effect. Recent ECB publications suggest around half of banks (by asset) are now expected to be at their preferred minimum levels of reserve holdings. Funding conditions have been adjusting to the removal of liquidity, primarily through the reduction in scarcity premium. As key thresholds are approached, the risk is for more volatility in short-term rates. The adjusted liquidity metrics suggest there is still scope for funding conditions to tighten more or faster than currently priced.
