For markets, the tail risk of a populist candidate winning the election adds a layer of uncertainty to an already fragile fiscal backdrop. The question is whether RN will be able to convey credibility regarding fiscal discipline, push business-friendly policies and soften its Eurosceptic rhetoric (France replaces Italy as European bond investors’ biggest worry, 27 Aug). Some investors we speak to draw a comparison between Le Pen and the Italian PM Meloni (Le Pen can run, but can’t hide her policy flaws, 8 Jul), who turned more market-friendly after her election. However, the French candidate remains closely associated with a populist agenda, given RN's electoral base draws significant support from low- and middle-income households (Radioscopie de l'electorat du Rassemblement National, 23 Jun), potentially creating pressure for policies involving higher public spending and purchasing-power support. This week also ended with the BLS publishing the prelimi- nary estimate of the 2026 payroll benchmark. It showed a 79k (178k private) downward revision to the March 2026 level of employment. The benchmark update won’t be finalized until early next year, and the key data used in the benchmark are likely to be revised up by then, which would yield a small positive revision. The key takeaway is that after a couple years of large downward revisions to employment, this year’s benchmark shouldn’t produce much net revision in either direction. records.text: ing captures the crowding dimension of a market, it does not directly observe whether prices are already moving in the direction the signal anticipates. To address this, we add a momentum signal as a confirmation filter and only trade the markets where both signals align. Specifically, we employ the delta-of-the-straddle signal across look-back windows of 32 days, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 2 years as described in Designing a Robust Trend Following System. At each weekly rebalance, we first identify the most over-owned (top 30% ) and most under-owned (bottom 30%) assets as before. We then apply the following filtering rule: • A long position (under-owned asset) is only retained if its momentum is positive, indicating that prices have already started to move up in line with the contrarian positioning view. • A short position (over-owned asset) is only retained if its momentum is negative, indicating that prices have already started to move down. Assets that fail the momentum check are dropped from the portfolio at that rebalance. The remaining names are sized using inverse-volatility weighting based on a rolling 1Y covariance matrix, with the overall portfolio scaled to an annualized volatility target of 10%. As in the baseline, we trade the front-month (1st generic) contracts exclusively, and we report both gross and net performance below. records.text: 6. UK budget still all about the macro. While there will be much more to say on policy specifics into the UK budget, the issue for Gilts remains a macro one. Namely, the level of headroom—the buffer against the balance budget rule—is low compared with the macro volatility that drives the headroom calculation. This suggests that fiscal policy decisions and as a result pressure on yields are tethered to energy prices, so it should be no surprise that the Gilt market remains the highest beta to global yield and energy developments. Higher energy prices will squeeze the UK budget via higher inflation and interest costs, complicating fiscal choices and driving higher uncertainty and risk premium. At the same time, lower energy prices provide breathing room under the current budget framework, and will allow a bigger compression of Gilt risk premium. We continue to forecast Gilt yields at 4.5% at year-end, but expect volatility to remain high, in contrast to Europe, which means our Gilt forecasts are a bit less bullish on a relative vol-adjusted basis (Exhibit 6). This points to upside risks to our forecasts, especially ahead of the upcoming budget, and undermines the case for belly or long-end Gilts, and so we continue to favor 2s10s steepening expressions. Empirical results In this section, we present the performance of the new skewness strategy by asset class and compare it with the corresponding performance of the trend-following strategy. We construct the skewness signal using lookback windows of 32 days, 64 days, 126 days, 1 year, and 2 years,7 and take the final signal as the average across these five windows. The position in each instrument is taken proportional to the skewness signal and inversely proportional to its volatility. The aggregate portfolio is dynamically risk- managed on an expanding-window basis, with an annualised portfolio volatility target of 10%. All performance figures are reported net of execution and replication costs. In equities, the skewness strategy achieves a respectable standalone Sharpe ratio of 0.32, though its positioning is materially long-biased. This reflects the well-documented tendency of equity returns to exhibit persistent negative realized skewness, which the signal harvests by going long. GDP, and are now higher than the primary deficit of $814bn (2.6% of GDP). 2025 was the first time that US interest payments were higher than the primary deficit and the trend is certainly not good. The CBO projects that net interest payments will top $2tr by 2035 (4.5% of GDP). Its 2026 projections, meanwhile, are based on an average 3m bill rate through the year of 3.3% and an average 10-yr yield of 4.1%. This is clearly a huge problem and, by showing his hand last week, Bessent has alerted the market to his concerns, leaving US duration an unattractive investment opportunity at current yield levels. Will the buybacks be enough to stem rising yields? Unlikely given it only increased the minimum buyback from $2bn to $4bn dollars. Over the quarter this is effectively an increase in buybacks in the 10-30yr area of the curve from $16bn to $32bn. Even then, it’s unlikely Treasury will accept $32b worth of par in offers. Given Q3 will see issuance in the 10yr+ part of the yield curve of $231bn, the extra $16bn in buybacks is the definition of a drop in the ocean. Increase market focus on a problem and then tackle it with a pea-shooter. Hardly the way to build confidence in US duration. August Tokyo CPI continues to accelerate; rice price drag emerges Tokyo core CPI accelerated to 1.8% y/y in August from 1.7% in July, while core-core CPI rose to 2.0%, returning to the 2% mark for the first time in four months. Strong inflation other than foods offset weaker energy prices, supported by higher imputed rents and household goods prices, including detergents, reflecting elevated naphtha costs. Overall, the data confirmed a gradual inflation pickup in line with the BoJ’s expectations and remains consistent with an early rate hike, though it does not materially strengthen the case for a September move. Is aging and population decline inflationary or deflationary? We view demographic aging as a potential source of inflationary pressure. Inflation ultimately reflects the balance between demand and supply. As the dependency ratio rises, the number of consumers grows relative to producers, causing demand to outpace supply. Aging is already contributing to labor shortages and could become a more pronounced source of inflation over time. The growing elderly population has increased labor demand, particularly in healthcare and nursing care services, where employment has expanded substantially. Meanwhile, Japan's working-age population has been declining since 1995. So far, rising labor force participation has largely offset this drag, but participation rates appear close to peaking while the decline in the working-age population is expected to accelerate. In the July nationwide CPI data, the contribution of bread products to overall CPI inflation rose to +0.03pp from -0.01pp in June. Numerous food price increases are scheduled from August onward ( Figure 9). In addition, as noted above, inflation pressure originating from crude oil prices is likely to persist for some time. By contrast, lower rice prices are set to weigh on CPI inflation from autumn through winter. Rice is purchased frequently, making its price changes highly visible to households. As a result, falling rice prices may not only lower CPI inflation but could also affect households’ perceptions of inflation and the inflation expectations emphasized by the BoJ. It will still take time for new- crop rice to become widely available. Meanwhile, it was reported on 26 August that the government is considering buying back around 150,000 tons of the reserve rice released in 2025 – roughly one-quarter of the total – during September 4 . This is equivalent to about 2% of annual demand and, if implemented, could mitigate the easing in supply-demand conditions to some extent 5 . Turning first to the data, the core PCE deflator rose 0.25%m/m (consensus: 0.1%) with small upward revisions to the prior three months, though portfolio management fees, which are subject to upcoming methodology revisions, made a large contribution to overall core. Notably, the market-based core measure that some FOMC members have preferred to look at rose just 0.15%m/m (see US: Profit / income ratio hits new record (PCE, GDP) , Abiel Reinhart, 8/26/26). The signal from jobless claims remains positive, signaling both stable job growth and downward pressure on unemploy- ment. Finally, markets read Warsh’s comments on Friday as hawkish, only exaggerating this flat- tening trend. Against this backdrop, 2- and 5-year yields rose 12bp and 6bp, respectively, while 10- and 30-year yields declined by 1bp and 6bp, respectively. Indeed, factoring in the growth in nominal GDP during this period, it might even seem contractionary at first glance. However, such a conclusion would be premature. That assessment relies on the unrealistic assumption that there will be no itemized requests and no supplementary budgets during the fiscal year. If itemized requests amount to several trillion yen, the FY27 budget would already be higher than the final FY25 budget (including supplementary budgets) at the initial request state. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Oil Tracker: Elevated Prices, Falling Inventories We continue to track the evolution of petroleum-product inventories, production, trade, and prices. The latest data suggest that crude oil inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell further, whereas total US crude oil and petroleum-product inventories edged higher. US domestic crude oil production remained broadly unchanged, while net imports of crude oil and petroleum products maintained their upward trend. Meanwhile, oil prices moved higher. As of August 21, US stocks of crude oil and petroleum products, which represent the EIA's estimate of how many barrels of crude oil and petroleum products are physically sitting in US storage at period-end, remained broadly unchanged from a week earlier. The stocks of crude oil in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) continued to fall to around 290 million barrels, the lowest level since April 1984. The Energy Department said the SPR's minimum inventory is determined by "cavern mechanics," which, when applied across the full system, translates to a conservative operational minimum of about 70 million barrels. If the SPR continues to decline at roughly its recent pace of 30 million barrels every four weeks, inventories would approach the operational minimum by the end of February 2027. records.text: European Economic Comment28 August 2026 ab 2 We expect German GDP growth of 1% this year and 1.5% next, with the fiscal stimulus contributing 60bp in both years. We see three macro implications/risks from the regional elections that could affect this view. First, that the government, in an effort to win back support, focuses even more on implementation of fiscal stimulus, which might help lift GDP growth and broader sentiment. Second, in the event that the coalition parties suffer heavy election defeats, they might interpret this as the result of the government's structural reform agenda presented in July, and hence choose to cut back reform ambitions in the parliamentary process in H2. This could entail, for example, keeping in place early retirement subsidies that otherwise are planned to be abolished. If this were to happen, the direct economic impact would likely be moderate (as we have not factored in a large growth boost from these reforms) even though it could dampen investor sentiment towards Germany. Third, we believe the fiscal expansion would be at risk only if the government were to break down and were no longer able to pass budgets, required every year to implement the fiscal stimulus. As noted above, this would presuppose an extreme scenario of Chancellor Merz calling, and subsequently losing, a confidence vote. He made no reference to long-term yields, JGB purchases or market-functioning considerations. His discussion of the underlying inflation trend was, however, more explicit. He broadened the focus from whether underlying inflation would rise to and stabilise around 2% to whether it could exceed 2%, adding that the Bank must be “more mindful than before of upside risks to prices”—a sentence absent from the baseline assessment in the July Outlook Report. The central message was therefore a firmer bias towards further policy normalisation, but without a commitment on timing: a higher hawkish boundary and a live-meeting signal, without a specified date. More than half of the speech was devoted to a point-by-point rebuttal of criticism surrounding the June hike, which lifted the policy rate to 1.00%, its highest in 31 years. records.text: Historical roll technicals We analyse in detail below how the indices have traded historically going into the roll for all rolls since 2017 (excluding 2020). The high-level takeaways are as follows: • CDX.IG, Main and Xover have typically tightened into the roll, with the main exceptions to this tightening bias coinciding with periods of elevated macro volatility. • CDX.HY, which rolls a week later than the other indices, does not display a clear pattern into its roll date. However, it does have a tendency to tighten into the roll date of the other indices, but to a lesser degree. • One of the most consistent patterns we have observed going into the roll is CDX.HY-CDX.IG decompression, with CDX.HY underperforming CDX.IG in 14 out of 17 rolls. Investor positioning into the roll Another important factor to consider going into the roll is current investor positioning. We show this for the latest data (21 August) in Figure 1 and compare this with what prevailed ahead of the prior roll in March 2026. We highlight some important features: • The Main roll looks set to be more "BAU" versus the previous roll, with $16bn longs, as opposed to a meaningful short-risk base in Main during the peak of the Middle East crisis in March. All else equal, this could make the roll flatter, as there are more longs than shorts to actively roll. records.text: 28 August 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 13 Facts vs. narrative Francis Yared | Strategist | +44-20-754-54017 Note: This note was originally published on 28 August 2026 We argued yesterday that an ECB terminal rate of 2.75% was plausible from both a bottom -up perspective (European data have been resilient) and a top -down perspective (the ~130bp differential to the US is consistent with historical reference points). Some have count ered that the spread to the US is too tight given the historical and prospective nominal GDP growth differential. The data suggest otherwise. Today’s CoTD shows the nominal GDP growth differential between the US and the eurozone. The historical average since 1999 is 1.2%, while the Bloomberg consensus forecast implies an average of 1.3% for 2026-28. The current terminal rate differential is ther efore consistent with both the historical and prospective GDP growth differentials. Moreover, medium -term tail risks could be skewed towards a tighter spread , given that: (1) US capex booms tend to be followed by busts , while AI capex in Europe has upside potential from a very low base ; and (2) a divided US government could force fiscal tightening, while German fiscal policy is likely to remain structurally easy for some time. records.text: tatistically significant upward trend in aluminium, consistent with broader momentum across the base metals complex (see Figures 1 and 2). Aluminium price has remained largely range-bound over the past month as the market balanced opposite supply-side dynamics. Above all, the lack of clarity regarding Alba and Qatalum smelters restarts has been offset by the recovery in North American production capacity and a clearer restart timeline for EGA. On top of that, geopolitical tensions in the Strait of Hormuz keep being a relevant catalyst, as the Middle East supply around 9% of the global aluminium output. Meanwhile, China has filled the gap, as primary aluminium exports has continuously surged since the beginning of 2026, partially offsetting Middle East supply loss. We see inventory contraction as the principal driver for aluminum's upward trajectory. This trend is underscored by declining LME stocks and is further amplified by a pronounced drawdown in Chinese inventories. Based on the above, we initiate a long position on the aluminium November 2026 contract and, as the deviation is not significant, we target the MarFA Macro upper band of USD3594.2/tonne with a notional size of USD5mn.

Figure 3: More long end liquidity support Source: State Street Markets, US Treasury Buybacks in focus: Treasury’s latest salvo in stabilizing yields has been through a series of buyback announcements. And while alterations to the buyback schema have generated a sizable market reaction, buybacks are not new. The program was formally introduced in the May 2024 Quarterly Refunding Announcement (QRA), which established both cash management and liquidity support buybacks. The latter are most relevant here, as they a re designed to support market liquidity by providing a regular and predictable mechanism for investors to sell off -the-run securities to Treasury. The evolution of this support has steadily evolved and expanded o ver the past two years , The initial program started with a $2 billion /per operation ceiling and a $30 billion per quarter cap, with full flexibility to allocate liquidity support throughout the curve. This was expanded to $4 billion per operation, with specific parameters established for long end operations (10-20y & 20 -30y) which targeted only $2 billion per operations/ a total of 4x per quarter. In late 2025 Treasury made further modifications, with an apparent focus on providing long end liquidity support. This is most obvious in banks that need to include accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) from changes in the fair value of AFS in their common equity tier 1 capital. The portion of those fair value changes attributable to interest rate moves that are hedged using PLM are accounted for in another line item (unallocated portfo- lio layer fair value hedge base adjustments) that offset the moves and dampen the impact on AOCI. The big question, then, is what can we determine about banks’ current usage of PLM from their filings? There are two main places to look, the 10-Qs/10-Ks and the call reports. After the introduction of PLM in 2022, a field was added to the call reports: “unallocated portfolio layer fair value hedge basis adjustments”. This field shows the amount of basis adjustments (applicable to the securities in a closed portfolio for the sake of PLM), that is, the adjustment to their fair value thanks to the PLM hedges that can’t show up in the individual line items. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 9 Exhibit 15: Cash withdrawals from the DHS - CBP , as a proxy for tariff refunds 0 20 40 60 80 100 120 140 Cash Withdrawals from DHS, CBP (Fiscal YTD, Bil $; 4-wk avg) Source: US Treasury, Haver Analytics, Morgan Stanley Research Tariff refunds represent cash returned to importers when customs duties were previously overpaid or later determined to be refundable, for different reasons, including a tariff exclusion or court-ordered refund or a drawback claim tied to goods that are exported or destroyed. The process generally runs through CBP, where importers or brokers submit the relevant claim and supporting documentation; CBP then reviews eligibility, confirms the entry and status, and certifies approved refunds for payment. In Treasury cash-flow data, we monitor these payments at high frequency through CBP-related withdrawals in the Daily Treasury Statement. We interpret this as a tariff-refund proxy.

records.text: 28 August 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week in review ECB accounts The ECB released the accounts of their July meeting this week. Our AI scored the Accounts of the July ECB meeting at 5/10 on the hawkish scale, slightly lower than the June meeting. Interestingly, while AI sees the hawkishness of the inflation discussion continuing to dominate, the hawkishness of the growth discussion is catching up. Our key takeaways from the July Accounts are consistent with a September hike and some risk of further tightening: (1) while the Governing Council remains data- dependent and not pre-committed, “another rate hike would likely be necessary unless the inflation outlook improved significantly”, (2) some Council members “would not have opposed” a hike in July and saw the need to move into “mildly restrictive territory”, (3) food price inflation is an upside risk, (4) “insurance hikes” are not ruled out, and (5) there is still a (relatively) dovish camp who saw a “strong” case for a pause and for whom second-round wage effects are a “low likelihood” event. Our baseline is a second and final hike in September to 2.50%, the upper end of the range of neutral. The risks are skewed towards the ECB hiking further into mildly restrictive territory. records.text: 2011. A couple of months ago , we argued that the comparison with 2011 was misplaced for three fundamental reasons. Firstly, the private sector is more resilient than it was in the aftermath of the GFC. Secondly, intra -EU divergences are smaller, as peripheral countries have significantly improved their external positions. Thirdly, on a forward -looking basis, fiscal policy is likely to ease rather than tighten, as it did post-2011. The data and market pricing have generally supported our view. Since then, the market has added ~25bp of additional tightening by the end of 2027. Yet, the eurozone composite PMI has risen by ~4pt. Our economists’ eurozone surprise index has reached a multi -year high. German GDP has been revised up. Bank lending conditions have tightened less than expected. The credit impulse has remained resilient. Last, but not least, one of the most cyclical indices, European banks, has outperformed its US peers. Looking beyond aggregate volumes, however, we find that segments where issuance has been heaviest relative to market size have also lagged. Supply remains a key focus for the market. As we head into the typically busy September issuance window, we take stock of issuance and performance so far this year. The €-IG market has absorbed more than €550bn of gross supply YTD, with an additional €260bn expected by year-end under our FY26 estimates. If realised, this would mark a record year for gross issuance. Yet, on the surface, the market has handled the supply well. Spreads remain tight at 78bp, almost unchanged from the start of the year, as higher all-in yields have provided strong technical support. The question is where the supply has landed, and whether any pressure points are emerging. Looking at the breakdown of senior issuance (we exclude subordinated debt, where issuance has picked up substantially this year), aggregate issuance patterns have not been especially unusual across either rating or maturity. There has been a small tilt away from the long-end in favour of shorter maturities, particularly the 5-7yr bucket (Figure 1), which is not very surprising in the context of much higher all-in yields. This left the level of GDP in 2Q slightly higher than previously reported. The expenditure breakdown showed a broad-based upturn after 1Q’s disappointing outturn. Deputy Governor Himino’s closely watched speech on 27 August featured notably hawkish remarks, including that “raising rates in a timely manner will help avoid inflation acceleration and abrupt rate hikes in the future. ” However, the market impact was limited, as expectations for a BoJ rate hike had already risen to the point that the OIS-implied probability of a September hike exceeded 80%. Against this backdrop, Governor Ueda was reported to be skipping the Jackson Hole symposium but attending the G20 meeting (Nikkei, 26 August). With expectations rising that he will meet US Treasury Secretary Bessent, communication from the BoJ will once again be in focus. With total amount of FY27 budget requests due to be announced in early September, but the scale of higher defense spending and item-based requests at the request stage reportedly remaining unclear (Reuters, 26 August), the results of the 10y and 30y JGB auctions will also be closely watched. The Twin Deficit score is a synthetic weighted average where we assign a higher weight to this year’s Twin Deficit (t), followed by gradually lowering the weights of the past five years (t-1, t-2, …, t-5) twin deficits and finally adding some weight to the cumulative Twin Deficit up to year t-5. This allows us to create a synthetic Twin Deficit score, which combines both the most recent flow and the historical stock of budget & current account deficits. While the LME copper price sits near USD6.3/lb, well above the government’s USD5.5/lb assumption, the underlying industrial reality is grim. Modern monetary theory (should have) laid to rest concerns about government debt in countries that issue in local currency, and while some exceptions exist, such as a euro area member that can issue in euros but cannot print them by fiat, the US is not one. Hard-currency debt, whether issued by an EM government or by a sovereign in the euro area, risks debt sustainability backlash much more so than local currency debt, meaning debt issued in the same currency as the sovereign controls, e.g., the US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and Japan. Exhibit 16 and Exhibit 17 show the evolution of EM hard-currency and local-currency bonds outstanding since the Great Financial Crisis (GFC). After the Greek debt crisis in 2012, EM countries issued more hard-currency debt than local-currency debt, increasing exposure to possible debt sustainability concerns. Since the pandemic, EM local-currency bonds proliferated. While issuer-related idiosyncrasies exist in EM, at the macro level, we think this development should reduce investor concerns of debt sustainability-related risk-off episodes in EM.

This is most obvious in banks that need to include accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) from changes in the fair value of AFS in their common equity tier 1 capital. The portion of those fair value changes attributable to interest rate moves that are hedged using PLM are accounted for in another line item (unallocated portfo- lio layer fair value hedge base adjustments) that offset the moves and dampen the impact on AOCI. Regression analysis of the type used in the IMF and Laubach papers also suffers from the absence of proper data. A proper analysis of the effect of debt accumulation on government bond yields requires a time series of investor expectations relating to government bond supply, not a semi-annual projection of 10-year forward federal government budget deficits from the CBO. Large deficits over short periods can produce inflation Of the four variables that matter, the speed at which the debt accumulates carries the clearest historical link to markets. We know how too large a deficit in too short a period of time can lead to runaway consumer price inflation. The post-pandemic period is "Exhibit A" (see Exhibit 34 ). The risk characteristics of the debt matter as well. We know how the average duration of the debt and the average coupon it pays can affect investor returns for the better, and worse. More importantly, the strength was broad-based: final domestic demand rose 3.9%Q SAAR, household consumption increased 3.3%, and fixed investment rebounded 5.3%. • Real consumption rose 3.3%Q SAAR versus the 1.7% pace embedded in the July MPR, with strength across services and durable goods. The saving rate also increased to 3.7% from 3.3%. • Private investment was another clear source of strength. Gross fixed capital formation rose 5.3%Q SAAR, with strength across machinery and equipment, residential investment, and non-residential structures, while government investment was a drag. • Trade provided a powerful boost. Exports surged 15.1%Q SAAR, broadly consistent with the strong rebound anticipated by the BoC, while imports rose just 1.1%. • Inventories substantially understated the underlying strength of the quarter. Inventory accumulation subtracted 4.9pp from annualized GDP growth as businesses drew down stocks following the 1Q build. Mechanically excluding this drag, growth would have been about 8.2%Q SAAR. • For the BoC, stronger activity data

While much of the focus of global rates markets has been on US and Japanese yields and policy responses, energy prices are still the main source of vol for European and UK rates (Exhibit 5). The drift to fresh highs in European gas alongside cyclical resilience and ongoing evidence of stronger German fiscal spending are likely to keep ECB hike risk beyond September in play. Unlike in the US and UK, where we expect the data flow to support an on hold Fed and BoE, we think that a September ECB hike will see EUR 2s5s out-flatten the US and UK curves. The ECB has the shortest fuse on inflationary risks among the major central banks, which we think will protect longer-dated forward rates in Europe vs other markets, including Japan. We expect Bund yields to drop modestly to 3.0% at end-2026, but volatility to remain low. This suggests that 5y5y rates in Europe remain a reasonable long, and help offset the negative carry shorting steep curves elsewhere, such as Japan. Sovereign credit in Europe should be able to weather modest ECB tightening beyond September, especially given the resilient growth backdrop. But the proximate risk comes from politics, especially for OATs where attention is already moving towards next year’s presidential election. records.text: Upgrading Our 2027 Margins Forecast Above Forwards We now expect 2027 diesel/gasoline margins vs. Brent to average at $63/$29/bbl in the US and $49/$22 in Europe, slightly above market forwards (Exhibit 10). A likely only gradual recovery in refinery runs will prevent large refined product stock builds as demand continues to recover. Lower realized and expected product stocks account for 50-70% of our 2027 diesel margins forecast upgrade (Exhibit 11). We also expect that the high forward-looking risk premium that is currently embedded in product margins will partially roll over to 2027 even if tensions in the Middle East deescalate. Elevated geopolitical uncertainty, likely persistent outages in Russia, and a steepening upward trend in global unplanned outages (Exhibit 12) will likely require a persistent risk premium to ensure adequate stocks, especially given the structurally tight refining fundamentals. We assume a $7-13/bbl risk premium for US/EU diesel margins in 2027, in line with a 50% chance that current unplanned refinery outages persist through next year. The decision to reduce EM carry exposure is driven primarily by Treasury Secretary Bessent’s recent announcement of long-end US Treasury buybacks, which are likely to ease financial conditions. If so, the Federal Reserve may ultimately need to offset this through a relatively tighter policy stance. Consequently, the near-term direction of the USD may hinge on Chair Warsh’s reaction function, potentia lly as soon as his Jackson Hole address on 28 August. Should Warsh refrain from signaling concern over easier financial conditions, USD weakness could persist, implying that the reduction in EM carry exposure was premature. Treasury had begun an open- ended series of auction size increases in August. At that quarterly refunding, TBAC was charged with examining the drivers of the rise in Treasury yields over the prior quarter. The presenting member highlighted that term premia had risen from historically low levels and that increasing Treasury supply likely contributed to the repricing. Higher growth expectations and a reassessment of the long-run neutral rate had also contributed. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. In particular, there is greater clarity into the budgeting process, with the large post -covid spending swings behind us. Additionally, while the Treasury Secretary continues to argue for lower long-term yields, greater reliance on the short end amongst stable policy rates also provides a bit more clarity on the funding front. Having said that, prudent fiscal management continues to require a buffer, which we estimate at approximately $800 billion based on Figure 9. From this perspective, we estimate that Treasury has a little over $100 billion in excess funding that can be used for buybacks. Growing deficit demands would nonetheless require that Treasury replenish these amounts in the near future given Washington’s inability to address its imprudent spending habits, which is the biggest investor concern as it relates to duration. records.text: at the end of this report. Key Takeaways USZ6 duration extends materially in a selloff as the CTD shifts toward longer duration bonds, creating a positively convex, payer like payoff. We value this additional convex payoff using a replicating portfolio, with cash bonds capturing duration risk and payer swaptions capturing convexity. The replicating swaption portfolio values the convex payoff at 12.4 ticks, versus just 8.7 ticks for net basis, implying the market prices it at 30% discount. Three unusual conditions make this opportunity possible: yields near the 6% notional coupon, wide basket coupon dispersion, and expensive payer skew. We recommend two trades to capture the underpricing of USZ6 convexity: buying USZ6 puts and buying USZ6 net basis through the current CTD. Part 2 presents a systematic approach to constructing weekly seasonality signals out-of-sample, and tests if these signals have held up over time on both a time-series and cross-sectional basis. The main G10 take-aways from the macro lens are that several consistent patterns come with credible explanations including SEK weakness in mid-Mar to Apr (dividends) and strength in late Dec (fiscal year-end), NOK weakness in Nov (oil), CHF strength in Jun/Dec (bank balance sheet repatriation), and NZD weakness in Aug (trade balance low). Main take-aways from the systematic lens are that trading seasonality systematically has not generated consistent returns over time. Our benchmark signals were generally effective in capturing FX cross-sectional returns pre-2020 (risk- adj returns: +0.37), but have yielded negative returns post-2020 (risk-adj returns: - 0.27). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 boom: the four-quarter change in nominal GDP is 6.6% against only 2.1% for real GDP. In 2Q 26, the disparity is even sharper, with nominal growth up 8.0% and real growth up only 1.5%, though much of the acceleration in the GDP deflator came from energy prices. Instead, what we believe is driving the improvement in corporate profitability is firm pricing power and margins: firms in the non-financial corporate sector have raised price per unit by significantly more than input costs have risen. As shown in Exhibit 4 , unit nonlabor and labor costs changed little in the second quarter and were offsetting on net. Firms pushed selling prices meaningfully higher with unit profits capturing the entire increase in per unit pricing. Higher prices plus unchanged costs equal high profits. We show the four-quarter change in per unit price, cost, and profits in Exhibit 5 . Over the prior four quarters, nonlabor costs have risen sharply, likely reflecting the increase in tariffs following Liberation Day in April 2025, and firms responded by holding down labor costs and raising prices well in excess of the increase in tariffs. In short, corporate sector profitability is booming because of pricing power and expanding margins, not because inflation is raising the nominal prices of input prices, wage costs, and output prices proportionately. So, we use the trend following signal to allocate between pure sectors. Sector-Factor mimicking portfolios First, we need to define pure sectors. Pure sectors are rooted in the exact same idea as pure factors1and are built the same way. So, pure sector-factor mimicking portfolios are sector portfolios that have an exposure of 1 to the targeted sector while having no exposure to other sectors, regions or factors. In the context of sectors, exposure is based on membership (not market cap weighted), albeit adjusted2 to deal with multicollinearity and thus differing from the often-used dummies of 1s and 0s. records.text: 22 Dobromir Tzotchev, PhD AC (44-20) 7134-5331 dobromir.tzotchev@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 28 August 2026 J P M O R G A N The Anatomy of a Momentum Crash Momentum drawdowns have a distinct anatomy. By decomposing prior crashes and overlaying the Quant Macro Index (QMI), we identify early-warning signals and regime vulnerabilities. Crowding rises 247.6% from T-6 to T-1, while volatility compresses 10.5%, building leverage just before dislocation. Momentum crashes are forecastable through crowding and acceleration signals, but only when interpreted through the macro regime lens. Figure 24: Crowding Path pre-Drawdown | MSCI GDM Source: J.P. Morgan Global Quantitative Strategy, Factset, MSCI. Curbing Momentum Drawdowns From diagnosis to action: can we translate the above insights into practical risk- management tools? We look at three progressively sophisticated risk-management tools: stoploss rules, volatility thresholds, and macro-based screening. Evaluated head-to-head across six regional universes, we find QMI Screening leads on Sharpe in five of six universes, V olatility Threshold dominates drawdown control, and Stoploss rules fail to top any category, confirming that reacting to realised losses is too late once pre- drawdown dynamics are in motion. Bottom Line: No single tool wins universally – QMI Screening for Return and efficiency, Volatility Threshold for Drawdown insulation, Stoploss for neither. We replicated that approach and incorporated some portfolio construction improvements in the April 2026 note when we systematically allocated between the sub-components of value. In the May 2026 note we took one more step toward generalization and building out the trend signal-based timing methodology within the pure factors space when we applied it to allocate systematically among pure sectors. Here we take the final step needed to close the loop, by applying trend-following to allocate among pure regions. Regions are similar to sectors, and different to factors, in that they are not expected to carry a positive risk premium — there is no economic reasoning to support why a region would out-perform another region over the long run, at least not in the same way we may expect, for example, value stocks to outperform the non-value counterparts. Furthermore, global regions are a zero sum game where one region’s performance gains are another region’s losses. We find increased noise levels as we seek to differentiate among regions. Top-down: The USD-EUR terminal rate differential is not particularly tight The USD-EUR terminal rate differential (proxied by Dec-27 SOFR versus €STR) is currently around 130bp. Is that too tight? Historically, the USD-EUR r* differential has ranged from -50bp to 250bp (HLW estimates). It tends to be tight during financial crises, as the US is more prone to boom/bust cycles, or when fiscal policy is relatively more expansive in Europe, as during the GFC, the 2001 dot -com bubble and the 1990s double whammy of German reunification and the S&L crisis in the US . Conversely, the spread tends to be wide during a capex boom , usually US -driven, or when the US has comparatively more expansive fiscal policy, as during the Reagan years. As such, markets are now pricing a ~60% chance of a hike in September, or nearly double what they were pricing before this speech, though there is still a fair bit of key data between now and the next FOMC meeting, namely the August employment and CPI reports. records.text: M Idea 22 Key Factors At The Core Of Our Sector Model We update the performance of the key factors underlying our sector model, in order of those weighted most highly to derive the top of our model (Exhibit 20 ), excluding those which we have already covered in the earlier methodology changes section. The line graphs demonstrates the pre-trade performance of the top versus bottom quintile or top and bottom versus the MSCI Europe index for each individual factor, rebalanced on a monthly basis. So for example for earnings revisions breadth, we would be taking the stocks with the most positive ERR in the last 75 working days vs those with the most negative ERR, tracking their performance for the month that follows on a daily basis, and then rebalancing once again at the start of each month. This is not to say that we recommend investors trade this way, but merely to show that factor performance and pre- trade Sharpe's indicate that ERR tends to be an indicator not just for past but also for future performance. Of course in our own sector model, we do not rebalance monthly but typically quarterly, towards the end of the earnings season where as many of the factors as possible are fully up-to-date (e.g. accruals and management sentiment score change are refreshed during earnings season). As Figure 13 shows, total outstanding marketable G4 government debt amounted to roughly USD 58tn at the end of 2025, with an aggregate WAM of 7.5 years. Around 57% of the debt stock matures within five years, while bonds with maturities above 10 years account for 24% of total outstanding debt. Private investors currently hold around 65% of all marketable government debt, with their ownership share reaching 75% in the front end (<1 year) and remaining elevated at 71% in the 10y+ sector . Despite substantial official sector participation in sovereign debt markets, private investors remain the dominant holders across all maturity buckets, including the long end of the curve. The maturity profile of holdings differs substantially across investor groups. We estimate the WAM of domestic central bank holdings at 7.7 years, compared with 8.0 years for private investors and 4.8 years for foreign official institutions. As a result, different official sector actions can have different implications for the maturity profile ultimately held by private investors. To illustrate this point, Figure 14 presents three simple scenarios. The scenarios are purely illustrative and are designed to highlight the directional impact of different official institutions’ actions on private sector holdings. The PASO system – mandatory open primaries held before the general vote – had been suspended for the 2025 mid-terms, with Congress approving the measure 43-20 in the Senate and 162-55 in the House of Representatives. Building on that precedent, the government sent a broader electoral reform bill to Congress in April 2026, seeking the permanent elimination of the PASO, alongside the adoption of a single paper ballot (Boleta Única de Papel) and a ‘Ficha Limpia’ provision barring candidates with criminal convictions from running. With the 2027 presidential race approaching, the stakes are high – eliminating the PASO would fundamentally reshape candidate selection dynamics and could benefit La Libertad Avanza, which lacks the party infrastructure of more established political forces. Congressional approval, however, remains uncertain, with significant resistance across the political spectrum. This parallels our trend-following signal in Designing robust trend-following system, which is based on a one-sample test of the mean: where the trend signal tests the first moment, the skewness signal tests the third. The aim here is illustrative—to enable a like-for-like comparison with trend-following by rooting both signals in the same hypothesis-testing logic—rather than to replace our existing skewness framework. Methodology A simple measure of distributional asymmetry is the sample skewness estimator b = m3 / s3, where m3 is the third central moment of returns and s denotes the sample standard deviation. To test the null hypothesis H0: γ₁ = 0 (no skewness, where γ₁denote the asset's true unobserved skewness), we rely on Fisher (1930), who showed that under normally distributed returns, sqrt(n)·b converges in distribution to N(0, 6). This implies that the standardized statistic Zskew = sqrt(n/6)·b is asymptotically standard normal under the null. As with any test statistic, a smaller absolute value of Zskew indicates weaker evidence against the null, while a larger absolute value signals stronger conviction that the distribution is skewed. records.text: Friday’s Preliminary Benchmark Revision to Payrolls: No Longer Negative On Friday at 10am ET (at the same time as Chairman Warsh’s Jackson Hole remarks), the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) will publish a preliminary estimate of the benchmark revision to the level of nonfarm payrolls for March 2026. The final benchmark revision will be issued and incorporated into nonfarm payrolls alongside the January 2027 employment report in February 2027. The key source data for the benchmark revision comes from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), which is derived from state unemployment insurance records. The March 2026 QCEW data will be released at the same time as the preliminary benchmark estimate, introducing uncertainty around the ultimate size of the revision. However, based on the nine months of data released since the last benchmarked period, March 2025, a modest upward revision appears likely. We expect a preliminary upward revision on the order of 50-450k (Exhibit 1), which would translate to a 5-40k upward revision to monthly payroll growth over April 2025-March 2026. A final revision of this magnitude would result in the average pace of payroll growth over April 2025-March 2026 being revised up from about 25k/month currently to 30-65k/month. The preliminary estimate for the benchmark revision will likely understate the final revision. Profit margins, which were already high post-COVID, advanced again to historically elevated levels. The link between profits and jobs in the midst of an expansion is somewhat loose, but strong profitability, which is going hand-in-hand with moderate labor costs, should provide room for firms to continue to grow hiring in the quarters ahead. At a minimum, the profit path is the opposite of a late-cycle compression brought about by rising wages. One caveat to this is that the largest source of profit growth is the technology sector, which is itself still shed- ding jobs. records.text: 27 August 2026 Fixed Income Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 17 Appendix A: Definition and methodology Twin deficits and twin deficits score: Twin deficits are one of our preferred measures of fiscal policy space. In addition to the conventional twin deficit calculation, which is simply the sum of the projected Budget & Current Account deficit of each country data from the IMF's World Economic Outlook (WEO) database, we have also created a "twin deficits score”. For each year, the twin deficits score is a weighted average of the previous years' twin deficits. We assign a higher weight to this year’s Twin Deficit (t), followed by gradually lowering the weights of the past five years (t-1, t-2, …, t-5) twin deficits and finally adding some weight to the cumulative twin deficit up to year t-5. This allows us to create a synthetic twin deficit score which combines both the most recent flows and the historical stock of budget & current account deficits. Considering the fundamental difference between Norway and other G10 countries, we make adjustments to Norway's twin surpluses and NIIP when mapping with its market pricing. Net international investment positions (NIIP): NIIP is a measure of a country's reliance on foreign funding and, empirically, it is highly correlated with 10-year and 30-year government bond yields in cross-sectional regressions. We anticipate a fundamental shift in BI’s approach now that Perry Warjiyo has been replaced as governor by Destry Damayanti. Under Governor Warjiyo, BI relied heavily on the high yields of Sekuritas Rupiah Bank Indonesia securities to attract foreign capital as well as on aggressively raising policy rates. We expect the new leadership to reduce reliance on SRBI issuance and focus on reduced FX hedge costs in the event of pressure on the currency. We expect this to reduce the outstanding amount of SRBIs. Currently, investor positioning is skewed toward short duration, with significant liquidity trapped in SRBIs. Local banks’ SRBI holdings are currently IDR621trn (see Figure 1). As SRBI issuance tapers under the new governor from twice a week to a biweekly schedule and with significant SRBI maturities approaching in October and November (Figure 2), we expect this sidelined liquidity to redeploy into the bond market, providing a tailwind for IndoGBs. The first SRBI issuance under the new governor, on 28 August, will be a critical litmus test for this thesis. However, as we flagged in the past two editions of this publication, the statistical significance of the relationship between month-to-date relative equity returns and month-end FX price action has been declining for months to current low levels (Figure 4T h e m o d e l ' s e x p l a n a t o r y p o w e r h a s d e c l i n e d ). As a result, even significant divergences in equity market performance fail to produce statistically robust FX trading signals. The direction of this month's signals, modest as they are, is itself a reason to question them. records.text: Trade Recommendations and Risks We still recommend that investors hedge geopolitical risks with deferred European diesel timespreads, and maintain our long Dec26-Mar27 European gasoil timespread hedging recommendation. The risks to our constructive deferred margins view are two-sided (Exhibit 14). If refinery outages remain at their 2026 peak and freight rates remain at current elevated levels (for instance, in a scenario of a prolonged Middle East conflict), we see US diesel margins remaining above $80/bbl through 2027 while European margins would average $16 above our baseline. Further escalation in refinery strikes in the Middle East and/or Russia may push both margins above $100 because markets tend to overshoot model-implied levels when stocks are especially depleted. We see a slower and more gradual demand recovery and a faster moderation in refinery outages as the main downside risks to our margins forecast. A 1mb/d decrease in refined product demand from potentially larger scarring, a faster normalization in Middle Eastern refinery runs by end-2026, and the related 50% decrease in the risk premium would push US/Europe diesel margins to $40/30/bbl by end-2027 — still above 2025 levels. Morgan Cross Asset Systematic Strategy Building top-down trend-followed pure sector portfolio In contrast to some of the common investment styles (factors), there is no investment reason as to why a sector should be expected to outperform others in the long run – no ‘sector risk premium’. Thus, there is no justification for asymmetric tilts here whereby no shorting would be allowed. With this in mind, we use a straightforward linear mapping mechanism where the [-1, 1] bound signal becomes the multiplier. Consistently with the approach used in recent monthlies, we first combine the pure sector portfolios using a risk budgeting approach which accepts each sector’s respective trend multiplier as input and uses this to tilt budget sizes relative to each other. Note that the symmetry discussed in the last section in regard to how sectors are tilted effectively ensures that there will be no performance flats – there is always a directional view for every sector. Q1: Is the euro area economy proving resilient to the energy shock? Strictly speaking, as a net energy importer the euro area should be highly exposed to the negative energy supply shock triggered by the Iran war. In any case, HICP inflation jumped to 3.0% in Q2, 1.2pp higher than expected at the start of the year. The household real income shock alone should have knocked more than 0.5pp off GDP. And yet euro area GDP was not weak in Q2, it was surprisingly strong. At 0.44% qoq, GDP growth exceeded expectations. We don’t have detailed components yet, but on the basis of available data household consumption grew despite the inflation shock. It is possible that elevated household savings buffered the real income shock on the assumption that it would be fleeting. There was also a targeted and temporary easing of fiscal policy (lower energy taxes), but this was not substantial and only moderated the rise in inflation slightly. That said, the euro area fiscal stance was already easy for 2026. Not nearly as easy as 2022, and skewed heavily towards Germany. But the stance is easy, not tight. Although BRL and COP also show strong fiscal vulnerability in Latam, we select MXN for our basket to avoid the high hedging costs and high idiosyncratic risks. PLN: Poland distinguishes itself in the CE3 by maintaining the loosest fiscal policy within the region (4% of GDP primary deficit), ranking quite high on our fiscal vulnerability index. Next year’s overall budget deficit will likely be close to 7% of GDP again and fiscal concerns could become more topical into the election at the end of 2027. CHF and NOK: Switzerland and Norway record the lowest fiscal vulnerability scores within the G10, with Norway exhibiting almost no fiscal risk. CZK: We favor long positions in CZK, given its low fiscal vulnerability and its historically mild reaction to US-centric fiscal risk-off shocks. The government has showed a preference to marginally loosen fiscal policy, but within the context of low debt/GDP and strong nominal GDP growth we think CZK will remain more insulated to moves higher in US term premium. records.text: 54 Dobromir Tzotchev, PhD AC (44-20) 7134-5331 dobromir.tzotchev@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 28 August 2026 J P M O R G A N An idealised daily reset skew-premium benchmark We first test the idea through an intentionally idealised one-day benchmark rather than an executable strategy. Each day, the backtest establishes a fresh one-month 25D gamma-neutral bull risk reversal, sells €100 million of payer notional, buys sufficient receiver notional to offset payer gamma and delta hedges the package with the on-the- run index. The structure is held for one trading session and fully reset the following day. Daily resetting keeps the strategy at a consistent point on the smile and prevents strike, maturity and Greek drift from accumulating. It therefore provides a relatively clean diagnostic of whether the implied-versus-realised skew gap appears in option P&L. Between September 2020 and July 2026, the idealised strategy generated steadily positive gross P&L, with a daily-P&L Sharpe of approximately 2.6 and relatively contained drawdowns. Drawdowns broadly coincided with periods in which realised skew spiked and spread-vol covariance was delivered. The gains were not evenly distributed through time. A substantial share accrued during 2022, when outright option volatility was elevated but the widening in Main spreads was relatively gradual rather than dominated by repeated spread-up/vol-up shocks. records.text: the Conference Board consumer confidence index edged down in August (from 90.2 to 89.4), but the present situation index rose nearly 7 points as households reported a better view of job conditions . Positively, the labor market differential improved to 7.5% from a cycle low of 2.7% in July, though this still lags levels observed late last year, when the unemployment rate was peaking (Labor confidence rises in Confer- ence Board report, Abiel Reinhart, 8/25/26). Turning to the housing market, new home sales fell 10.5% m/m in July, the slowest since January, reflecting continued demand pressure from elevated mortgage rates and afford- ability constraints despite ongoing builder incentives . Inventories stayed high , with homes available for sale rising to 488k from 479k and months’ supply climbing to 9.6 from 8.5, remaining near the upper end of the cycle range. Softer demand flowed through to pric- ing, with the median transaction price down 0.9% y/y (New home sales fall to six-month low in July, Bennett Parrish, 8/25/26). The prelim July durable goods report showed continued solid growth in key categories. Total durable goods orders rose 1.1% m/m, led by a 10.6% increase in the aircraft segment (ex-transportation, orders increased 0.4%). One interpretation holds that the deluge of corporate debt has crimped demand for long- term US government debt and sent yields higher than the US administration would like. What the running mates reveal: The vice-presidential picks tell two different stories about each campaign's strength. Lula’s choice was no choice at all; keeping Alckmin signals continuity and confidence in a formula that has already succeeded. Flávio Bolsonaro’s process, however, was the opposite: a month-long scramble that exposed significant weaknesses in his coalition. Because the Centrão parties (União Brasil, Progressistas and Republicanos) all declared neutrality in the presidential race, Bolsonaro was forced to build a ticket entirely from within his own party (PL). This decision cost him the extra TV and radio time that allied parties would have provided. On the final day of the conventions, Bolsonaro named Gaspar – best known as the rapporteur of the social security (INSS) corruption inquiry (CPMI do INSS) – passing over the female candidates his camp had floated for weeks in a bid to court women voters. Lula therefore enters the race with a settled, broad-front ticket, and more TV and radio time, which could be an edge in a very tight race. The race begins: The electoral campaign officially started on 16 August, with mandatory TV and radio ads starting on 28 August. Jobless claims remained upbeat in the latest report, signaling both stable job growth and downward pressure on unemployment. Initial claims for the week ending August 22 fell to 203k from 207k the prior week and continue to run well below year-ago levels. Con- tinuing claims for the week ending August 15 (the payroll and household survey reference week) fell 18k, continuing to run below the same month in 2023, when the unemployment rate was 3.7%. That points to downward pressure over time on unemployment, though the higher number of long-term unemployed now means that the rate shouldn’t be expected to immediately fall towards those earlier levels (More good news from claims, Abiel Rein- hart, 8/27/26). records.text: 36 Dobromir Tzotchev, PhD AC (44-20) 7134-5331 dobromir.tzotchev@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 28 August 2026 J P M O R G A N Recently,several risks materialized for FX carry: Brent slid from near 100 to about 80, Nasdaq fell roughly 10% before rebounding, and we saw an historical intervention to support Yen. Despite this toxic mix, carry drawdowns were modest: global risk- adjusted, global real, and G10 risk-adjusted baskets fell about 1–2% from the peak, while value baskets rose 1.7%/2.2% for Global/G10 portfolios. Carry losses were driven by JPY , with no real contagion. Last week’s move was nowhere near summer 2024 carry deleveraging, when the global risk-adjusted basket dropped about 7% from mid-July to early August and the entire FX cross-section priced a broad unwind. This time, high-yielders held up and low-yielder repricing stayed contained, suggesting carry resilience and supporting a still-bullish stance on global baskets. We are more cautious on carry restricted to G10, albeit still positive, given the long AUD and NOK exposure to energy volatility. Regarding other signals, it is worth mentioning that growth momentum baskets continue to trade strongly this year for both Global/G10 portfolios, especially based on Economic Activity Surprise Indices (Global/G10 EASI-based growth momentum up 7% and 4% YTD). Term premium analysis suggests that Japanese cash and swap 5s10s term premia remain elevated, while Swiss and US term premia appear compressed. While seasonal patterns point to higher term premia into autumn, macro developments are likely to remain the dominant driver. Inventories moved sharply in the opposite direction, subtracting 4.9pp from annualized GDP growth. Businesses shifted from accumulating inventories in 1Q to drawing down stocks in 2Q, including significant withdrawals by manufacturers, wholesalers and farm operators as well as gold and precious-metal inventories. records.text: nd the curve evolve, USZ6 will converge toward a specific CTD, while the replicating portfolio reflects the current probability weighted distribution of potential CTDs. The two will therefore diverge over time. Importantly, the swaption portfolio loses value through time decay, while the convex payoff from CTD switching does not decay in the same way. Our swaption based estimate may therefore understate the value of the convexity embedded in USZ6. We construct the replicating portfolio to match the payoff of a short position in one USZ6 contract as follows: • The cash component is a $115,075 notional short position in the 4.75% Nov43s. We use Nov43s because they are the expected CTD across most rally scenarios. We size the position using the conversion factor so that its risk closely matches USZ6 in a rally. • The residual payoff between USZ6 and the Nov43s is convex and resembles the payoff of a payer option. We approximate this convexity using a portfolio of SOFR payer swaptions with varying notionals, recognizing that some swap spread risk remains. • Exhibit 5 compares the residual payoff between USZ6 and the Nov43s with the payoff of the replicating swaption portfolio across instantaneous rate shocks. • Swaption notionals are chosen to provide the best fit to the residual payoff. Swaption expiries are set to Dec 31, 2026 to be consistent with the last delivery date of USZ6, and underlying swaps are 5Jan27 -> 15Nov43 to be consistent with the cash bond.

Key Takeaways We remain of the view that late 2027 early 2028 ECB pricing is too high as we do not see the need for monetary policy to be in restrictive territory after the energy shock dissipates. We are broadly neutral on long-end duration, and we are still recommending forward steepeners with the 3y2y/10y5y being our favorite expression. In EGB/SSAs, we re-enter short in France vs EU and keep short in Austria vs the Netherlands and short Belgium vs Ireland. We stay neutral on Italy. Swap spreads up to RX can continue to range trade and RX-UB boxes will remain curve proxies. We still see value in €str/6s wideners in the intermediate part of the curve. The reason for Bessent’s extended involvement is fairly clear to us, to limit Japan’s selling of Treasury securities, whose funds may be needed to support the MOF’s intervention aspirations. The additional suggestion that the Fed expand its FIMA limits to allow foreign officials to repo even more UST and we get a glimpse into Bessent’s true motivations. records.text: erable to escalating global concerns around fiscal deterioration – and identify potential trade ideas that tap into those findings. First, we identify fiscal vulnerabilities through a fiscal scorecard and forward-looking local debt dynamics across EM and DM economies. We then evaluate currency reaction functions by analyzing historical responses to fiscal-risk shocks. Finally we construct a risk-weighted FX basket that integrates these metrics while minimizing the negative carry profile. We evaluate the fiscal vulnerability of DM and EM economies using debt sustainability metrics (see Figure 1) and the metric for the budget deficit adjustment required in 2027 to keep the debt-to-GDP ratio constant, which captures the gap between the projected primary deficit and the ‘natural’ growth rate of debt/GDP for each country (Figure 2). This indicator helps us to gauge near-term debt sustainability from a forward-looking perspective. We identify the USD, JPY, CAD, HUF, BRL, PLN, ZAR, MXN, and COP as the currencies most vulnerable to those growing fiscal concerns. To assess whether these vulnerabilities are already priced in, we analyze their current term premiums in local curves and asset swap spreads. While most fiscally vulnerable currencies exhibit elevated term premiums and wider asset swap spreads relative to historical averages, the HUF, CNH and ZAR appear to have comparatively low risk premia priced (see Figure 4 in Appendix). records.text: he Adorni episode (Figure 16), yet it remains above where Fernández and both Kirchner administrations stood at the same point in their terms, and close to Macri’s at the same stage (Figure 17). The October mid- terms last year won by the government showed that the government still has support. What matters for the reform agenda (see page 9) is that the floor has so far held: erosion is the norm, and the government retains more political room than the recent drawdown implies, as long as it remains more willing to negotiate with governors than it did in 2025. Election anxiety: The risk is that another similar-sized leg down in popularity – possibly driven by the weak domestic consumption, declining purchasing power and cool labor market – would close that gap well before next year’s election. This could lead to further uncertainty about Milei’s re-election in 2027, the future of the current stance of the fiscal accounts and of the reforms being implemented this year. Andrew Fu | Strategist | +1-212-250-1743 Note: This note was originally published on 25 August 2026 Yesterday morning, senior Treasury officials indicated that increases in Treasury’s long-end buybacks could be funded through the TGA as opposed to bill issuance. Mechanically, TGA-funded buybacks would initially increase reserve balances as Treasury cash is transferred into the private sector . However, in response to the influx of reserves, the New York Fed’s Open Market Trading Desk would likely do fewer reserve management purchases (RMPs) than otherwise. This effectively keeps buybacks as a “twist” operation functionally identical to buybacks funded by bill issuance, though with the caveat that RMPs are conducted in off-the-runs compared to on-the-run issuance so the market impact may differ slightly. While the announced buyback sizes are far too small to have any immediate impact on front-end dynamics, if conducted in large enough size over a sustained period, the shortening of issuance maturities could eventually spill over into funding conditions as excess bills may crowd out overnight borrowing from MMFs. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real time information on consumer behaviour. records.text: Global Precious Metals Comment27 August 2026 ab 2 Global Precious Metals Comment UBS Research Act I — fundamentals restore the floor Positioning was exceptionally lean heading into the August rally. Investors were reluctant to buy the dip while persistent inflation kept the risk of renewed Fed tightening alive, but there was equally little conviction behind building large outright shorts. Despite a roughly 30% retracement from the year’s highs, medium- and long-term sentiment remained constructive, with many investors waiting for a better level and clearer signals to start rebuilding strategic exposure. Repeated failures to sustain a move below the psychological $4,000 level gradually restored confidence. Evidence that official-sector buyers were using lower prices to increase purchases reinforced that floor: aggregate central-bank buying rose as prices fell, with China particularly notable. Physical flows were also more resilient than we had expected. China’s imports remained well above both last year’s pace and historical averages. India’s imports continued to face regulatory headwinds, but seasonal patterns appear to be asserting themselves. Taken together, these trends point to stronger fundamental demand support through the second half and into the festive season. Soft US data provided the catalyst in early August, prompting markets to scale back Fed hike expectations. records.text: Global Macro Strategy - Views and Trade Ideas 27 August 2026 Citi Research 10 Until November, what other tools can they use? How much TGA firepower? Recent press reports (CNBC, 24th Aug) saying that the Treasury could use its general account (TGA) to fund bond purchases have caught the market’s attention. While there are no details of the size or scope, such a move would increase bank reserves, all else equal. This can provide a boost to risky assets. In terms of the mechanism, our colleagues note from early 2022 outlines how: QT, or not QT? RRP is the question. Empirically, we have argued that central bank liquidity (i.e. changes in bank reserves) has become less important as central banks have moved to conventional monetary policy via the level of interest-rates. This is shown in Figure 23, where equities have delivered positive returns in the last few years even as bank reserves have declined gradually. Using higher frequency weekly correlations, we can see the picture is more nuanced, with the time-varying correlations (rolling 26w) with risky assets picking up in recent months. This suggests that a TGA drawdown, should one occur, would provide a boost to risky assets. However, in the base-case, our Rates Strategy colleagues do not think the TGA target balance (of 5 days coverage of government operations) will change. We always thought that consumers would smooth the inflation shock by (at least temporarily) lowering their saving rates so that private consumption would not react 1:1 with the drop in real income. Still, consumers have been more resilient that we expected. One factor here has also been that household’s consumption of motor fuels (which brings little value added to the economy) has dropped massively. Whether this stays like that or whether consumers need to adjust progressively other parts of their basket if prices remain elevated is still an open question. In our modelling, a shock of 1% to households disposable income takes around four quarters to make its way into meaningfully lower private consumption. A number of reasons have n contributed to the Dollar’s tough summer as we discussed last week, with policy volatility being a common factor. First, small but unusual US interventions in the Yen and Treasury markets have shown a clear revealed preference for supporting other assets, even at the cost of Dollar weakness. Second, beyond that signal, and each individual action, this greater willingness to resort to unconventional choices raises questions about whether other even more extreme choices that come at the expense of the Dollar could be considered, especially if other harder choices on fiscal and monetary tightening are avoided. And third, the opacity of the Fed reaction function, against a backdrop where inflation data has been a touch more quiescent, has added to near-term pressures on the Dollar. Chair Warsh took the opportunity to address the last of these in his Jackson Hole speech, and he laid out some monetary policy principles and a hawkish assessment of recent inflation readings that should keep some hike premium in September and for the rest of the year. In addition, near-term cyclical considerations are more supportive for the Dollar. More broadly, while CEE currencies sold-off, the Euro and other European currencies, such as SEK, were mostly flat. In our view, this relative CEE underperformance is not fully consistent with the economic and geopolitical implications that a conflict escalation would have in Europe, and therefore, should not be sustained. Prior to these headlines, HUF had been appreciating and outperforming its regional peers, consistent with our view that the Forint could catch-up after underperforming in prior weeks, and our open trade recommendation to be short PLN/HUF. Also this week, the MNB cut rates by 25bp in line with expectations, but stopped short of guiding for a continuation of cuts in September. We think Governor Varga’s comments on the inflation target revision, and that the results could be published in the autumn, were the most important takeaway from the meeting. This is because we have been expecting local catalysts—including the inflation target revision, but also the Euro adoption plan, the 2027 budget, and the disbursement of EU funds—to drive HUF stronger later in the year. Looking ahead, if geopolitical concerns ease, we expect HUF to return to its relative outperformance, especially as local catalysts begin to unfold in Q4. records.text: an On the policy front, Director Pulte’s LLPA tweet might promise a little more excitement (“We are nearing the end of our review of certain LLP As. Decisions coming soon.”). The Director has been talking about LLPAs since his confirmation hearing, and so the precise timing is hard to know. But we lean towards thinking that the grids will be steepened, with a reduction in cross-subsidy and less focus on making ‘affordable’ loans. For much of the last half decade, the GSEs raised base g-fees while waiving LLPAs for a sizeable share of their book that fell below specific income thresholds (Figure 4B a s e g - f e e s r o s e a s c r o s s - s u b s i d i z a t i o n o n t h e b o o k i n c r e a s e d ). As a result, the cross subsi- dy has been even larger than what the base grid would imply. By tweaking this formulation, the GSEs could either increase the revenue they earn on those loans or just cede that part of the footprint to FHA. In Japan, an earlier hike would be a welcome step for long-end stabilisation, but the hurdle to out-hike the front-end remains high. Our Japan team’s recent BoJ forecast revisions are close to market forwards, but the precedent of a September hike would likely keep belly rates rising in the near term. We now expect 10y JGB yields at 3.0% by year-end, from 2.5% currently, as the market is likely to keep pricing risks of further hikes until the fiscal and inflation outlook becomes clearer. This implies a path for real rates that we think will prove to be unsustainable in Japan, pointing to increasing asymmetry towards lower 10y yields vs the current forwards. Weights will be higher (lower) with Anthropic share price Another piece in the NDX puzzle: Anthropic will likely enter NDX on the close of its 15th trading session: at ~1.3% weight. Given the 3x float implementation, Anthropic will then likely scale quickly to its full potential weight upon share unlocks. Anthropic inclusion into NDX should initially drive a very small 10-20bp volatility bump. This tends towards 60bp as the float increases towards 100%. However, it’s worth noting that the NDX December reconstitution could offset that bump. A software (IGV) story: Anthropic also could be eligible to enter IGV (SPNASEUT) as soon as December, conditional on: 1) S&P TMI inclusion (expected on day 5); 2) a GICS Sub-Industry of Application or Systems Software; and 3) float of >20% of market cap (see S&P North American Sector Indices Methodology). The percentage float seems the most likely blocking point. This could push inclusion into March 2027. Once eligible, Anthropic would likely enter IGV at a capped weight of 8.5%. The impact on IGV volatility is ambiguous. Assuming (~70% IV) at the time of inclusion, all else equal this bumps IGV vol 1.5pts. However, the theme of AI disruption (Anthropic versus traditional software) suggests Anthropic might be extremely decorrelated versus other IGV members, negating much of the impact. * Current members sorted by Market Cap. records.text: 28 August 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 28 FAQ on German federal states Note: This note was originally published on 26 August 2026. How large is the German federal state bond market? The German federal state bond market amounts to EUR 460.3bn in total (as of 24 Aug), with 97% denominated in EUR, 2% in USD and all other currencies accounting for less than 1%. EUR 406.5bn of the outstanding federal state bonds are denominated in EUR and have an outstanding volume of at least EUR 500m. Seven out of the 30 largest EUR denominated SSA issuers in terms of outstanding volume are German federal states, showing the importance of federal states in the EUR denominated SSA market: NRW EUR 122.6bn, Berlin (BERGER) EUR 53.7bn, Lower Saxony (NIESA) EUR 47.9bn, HESSEN EUR 40.5bn, Baden -Wuerttemberg (BADWUR) EUR 26.5bn, Rhineland -Palatinate (RHIPAL) EUR 21.6bn and Schleswig-Holstein (SCHHOL) EUR 21.2bn. Do federal state bonds benefit from an explicit guarantee by the federal government? There is no explicit guarantee by the federal government for debt of federal states (or their municipalities). However, we are not aware that sub -sovereigns in any other country benefit from an explicit guarantee from the central government. In our view, an explicit guarantee for sub-sovereign issuers which investors can use in court as a legal claim against the central government would be very unusual, particularly in case of a federal republic like Germany.
