records.text: ereign issuers which investors can use in court as a legal claim against the central government would be very unusual, particularly in case of a federal republic like Germany. Do German federal states benefit from the same regulatory treatment as Bunds? In line with Bunds, bonds issued by federal states are 0% risk weighted under EU CRR, qualify as LCR level 1 assets under the EU LCR Delegated Act, and have a stress factor of 0% (spread and concentration risk) under EU Solvency II. However, being in category II (instead of category I), federal states have a slightly higher haircut than Bunds at ECB repo transactions (link and link). Why do German federal states (and municipalities) benefit from the same risk weight and LCR eligibility like Bunds? EBA provides lists of regional governments and local authorities (RLGs) for which a 0% risk weighting applies (link). This list refers to RLGs for which Article 115 (2) CRR applies (link). In case of Germany, the list just mentions “All” instead of listing specific names of German RLGs. This means all German federal states and all their municipalities are 0% risk weight in the EU, in dependent from their rating (or if they do not have a r ating). As Article 10 of the EU LCR Delegated Act ( link) refers to Article 115 (2) CRR, these 0% risk weighted RLGs are LCR level 1 eligible in the EU. Find more FAQ in the full comment (link). records.text: y of Finance, Deutsche Securities Mapping the Budget into JGB Issuance From the perspective of JGB supply and demand, the headline size of the general account is less consequential than the three principal variables into which it ultimately translates. The first is the amount of new JGB issuance determined when expenditure and revenue are reconciled in the year-end initial budget. The second is the aggregate size and maturity composition of the JGB Issuance Plan published concurrently. The third is the funding mix employed for any supplementary budget during the fiscal year. FY2026 provides a useful point of reference. Notwithstanding an initial budget of approximately JPY122.3tn and record projected tax revenue of JPY83.7tn, new JGB issuance increased for the first time in five years, to JPY29.6tn. Total issuance amounted to JPY180.7tn, including JPY135.8tn of refunding bonds and JPY13tn of FILP bonds. In FY2027, the expenditure floor rises to JPY135tn, while the reduction in the consumption-tax rate on food creates an annual revenue shortfall of JPY5.8tn. The prime minister has pledged to avoid financing the measure through deficit bonds, although no corresponding funding package has yet been specified. Even after allowing for the natural growth of tax revenue, an increase in new issuance into the JPY30tn range appears highly probable; the extent of the upside will depend upon the manner in which the revenue shortfall is addressed. Eurozone HICP: Headline +0.3pp to 3.2%, core -0.1pp to 2.4% While we previously thought inflation had peaked in May at 3.2%, we now forecast headline inflation to rise by 0.3pp to 3.2% y/y in August (out on 1 September), returning to its May level. The increase is expected to be driven entirely by higher energy inflation (+3.5pp to 13.8% y/y), more than offsetting a slight easing in core inflation (-0.1pp to 2.4% y/y) and stable food inflation (1.2% y/y). Within core inflation, we expect services inflation to edge down 0.1pp to 3.2% y/y, while goods inflation is likely to tick up by 0.1pp to 1% y/y. At the country level, we forecast inflation to rise in Germany (+0.2pp to 3% y/y) and Italy (+0.3pp to 3.2% y/y), while remaining unchanged in the Netherlands at 3% y/y. The flash estimate for France came in line with our expectations, rising 0.3pp to 2.7% y/y, while inflation in Spain was slightly stronger than expected, increasing 0.6pp to 4.5% y/y (UBSe: 4.4% y/y). Looking ahead, we expect Eurozone inflation to hover around 3%-3.1% y/y for the rest of the year. Overall, we expect inflation to average 2.8% in 2026 before slowing to 2.4

In this weekly, we turn to the remaining questions on what households want from the forthcoming Budget. 1. Britons back Burnham’s devolution. In a convincing backing of Burnham’s devolution drive, 41% of households surveyed agreed that more decisions about how England is governed should be made outside of London (net balance: +21%). This tend ed to resonat e more strongly with the young (where support for devolved economic policy rose to 45%). Breaking our responses down by income group, it was the low- and high- income groups (< GBP 20k and >50k) that reported relatively high support for devolution. Long -end buybacks regularly attract as much as $20bn in offers, giving Treasury substantial scope to increase operation size in the near term. Going a step further, Treasury could maintain operational flexibility by releasing its updated buyback schedule without specifying long -end operation sizes, instead providing that information in the formal buyback announcement the day before the operation. This would make the buyback program less predictable, while substantially raising the hurdle for investors to short the long end. A more interventionist approach would be to make buybacks more responsive to market conditions. Treasury could justify it by emphasizing that buybacks are a liquidity-management tool, and that temporary factors such as large corporate issuance and illiquid summer trading can impair market functioning, pointing to the recent rise in long-end yields as supportive evidence. An extreme approach would be to tie buybacks to some implicit level of yields, with operation sizes responding to yields above certain thresholds. We view the likelihood of this as low, as markets would likely interpret it as an unofficial form of yield curve control and challenge it if they view that Treasury lacks the capacity needed to credibly commit to yield targets. Sizing matters more than the precise strike choice, with gamma-neutral sizing providing the cleanest tested exposure to the difference between skew carry and realised spread-vol covariance. The strategy nevertheless remains exposed to meaningful tail and implementation risks. It is short vanna and loses during abrupt spread widening accompanied by sharp volatility increases. It can also lose through adverse skew steepening as the options age, even when realised spread volatility remains relatively contained. Importantly, all results reported here are gross of transaction costs. Bottom line Taken together, the two pieces suggest that Main option skew embeds a persistent spread-vol covariance premium and that this gap is visible in gross risk-reversal P&L. A short-payer/long-receiver structure earns theta for supplying risk-off protection while bearing short-vanna and skew-steepening risk, with gamma-neutral sizing providing the cleanest exposure among the implementations tested. The key remaining question is how much of the premium survives realistic transaction costs and portfolio implementation. From smile dynamics to a potential skew premium CDS option skew is the static market footprint of a dynamic relationship between spreads and volatility. Wider spread strikes generally trade at higher implied volatility, reflecting the greater value attached to option protection in risk-off states. The important empirical question is therefore not simply whether payer volatility is expensive relative to receiver volatility, but how much of the spread-volatility co-movement embedded in the smile subsequently realises. Our Credit Volatility Field Notes addressed this question using the skew stickiness ratio, or SSR. Fresh foods, LHS) Other foods (LHS) Rice (RHS) %y/y Source: MIC Is aging and population decline inflationary or deflationary? We view population decline itself as neither inherently inflationary nor deflationary, whereas population aging can be inflationary. Inflation and deflation fundamentally reflect the balance between demand for and supply of goods and services. As population aging increases the dependency ratio, the number of people consuming goods and services rises relative to the number producing them. As a result, demand may increasingly exceed supply, creating inflationary pressure. By contrast, population decline does not necessarily affect inflation if the decline reduces both consumers and producers proportionately. The impact ultimately depends on the accompanying changes in demographic structure, but population decline by itself does not automatically generate either inflation or deflation. Is population aging already exerting inflationary pressure today? In practice, this is increasingly manifesting itself through labor shortages and may become a more explicit source of inflationary pressure in the future. CEE: Most, but not all, pieces fit. The CEE currencies traded weaker this week n following reports of a potential escalation in the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Given the geographic proximity and risks of hybrid attacks, it makes sense for these currencies to underperform, especially as we had previously argued that there was no ‘conflict’ premium embedded in these currencies. The relative performance ranking—with HUF moving the most, followed by PLN, and CZK depreciating the least—is also consistent with historical parallels and respective risk betas. Moreover, Hungary is still heavily reliant on Russian oil and gas imports, and so any potential withdrawal of supply would have meaningful implications for Hungarian growth and external balances.

As a result, it they were to deploy their remaining $100+bn of cap space into the market over the couple of months remaining before the midterms, they might be able to temporarily compress spreads—but any gains would be short lived and probably met by a decent amount of selling. Lifting the portfolio caps (which would require the consent of both Treasury and FHFA) might increase the impact, though the stability vs. cost of funding considerations (i.e. terming out debt vs. funding everything short) make that path unappealing for other reasons. All in all, we think it’s going to be difficult to meaningfully reduce mortgage rates ahead of the midterms. The government estimates operating expenses at 18.5% of GDP, followed by interest payments at 4.4% of GDP, while investment remains at 4.1% of GDP. The administration under new President Abelardo de la Espriella faces an uphill battle in passing the new Adjustment Law due to its low congressional presence, with no seats in the Lower House and only four in the Senate. Congress is highly fragmented (Figures 5 and 6), with Centro Democrático (former President Alvaro Uribe’s party) holding 17 Senate seats and Pacto Histórico (the opposition party of de la Espriella’s immediate predecessor Gustavo Petro) controlling 25 out of 42. This forces the government to rely on negotiations with Centro Democrático, the Liberal Party, the Green Alliance and other smaller factions. The inputs for this methodology won’t capture structural features or bugs (like rent control) but can be used to identify markets that are hitting their nadirs. Lenders and bond investors may care more about the cross-sectional analysis, though they shouldn’t ignore the self-history approach. Equity aims for upside while debt aims to preserve princi- pal and earn a coupon. Cross-sectional analysis can help identify better markets to lend to today in relation to others, but lenders should also be cognizant of whether the markets are caught in a down or updraft. Are you lending to a market that is cross-sectionally strong today but one that is worsening against its own history? Ideally, lenders should consider markets where the cross-sectional rankings are relatively strong and the self-history scores are bottoming out or improving. records.text: Lee Ferridge 26 August 2026 1 Insights Classification: General, Complimentary Material DM FX Weekly : Beam yields u p , Scotty? US Treasury Secretary Bessent last week managed to create a mini-crisis all of his own doing. By the surprise announcement that he was intending to increase the size of long-end Treasury buy-backs to $4bn from $2bn he highlighted to the market how concerned he was about rising yields. With the 30-yr last week reaching its highest yield since 2007 one can perhaps understand the worry, but the announcement (and subsequent TV appearances) only served to highlight the problem. This week we take a look at the implications for FX markets, in particular the US dollar. The broad conclusion? Well, we remain underweight the USD in our portfolio. Does that answer the question? We also maintain our CAD long versus the AUD. There is plenty of opportunity for more U-turns before meaningful trade sanctions are imposed on January 1st 2027. This week’s CAD reaction seems, to us at least, an over-reaction. High-income homeowners may be staying put, but they do not appear to be renovating at a pace sufficient to offset other drags. And, as noted earlier, growth in improvement spending has been highly procyclical, closely following existing home sales with a lag. Indeed, existing home sales enter JCHS’s LIRA model with a five- quarter lead. The persistent weakness in sales therefore helps explain why improvements spending has remained weak. This low pace of housing turnover has been abetted, in turn, by elevated financing costs. The financing constraint High mortgage rates have weakened improvement spending through two channels. Mortgage rates have remained above 6% since the Fed’s hiking cycle and have risen another 55bp over the past six months (Figure 7). A layer-by-layer look at bank PLM activity In this piece, we’ll go into detail on banks’ usage of the portfolio-layer method (PLM) hedg- ing and what we can (and can’t) determine from the various disclosures in quarterly filings and the call reports. Prior to PLM, banks had some limited ability to hedge prepayable assets through last-of-layer, but the introduction of PLM and the sell-off in 2022 spurred more banks to consider hedging AFS securities while receiving beneficial accounting treatment. We can see that the amount of bonds included in closed portfolios for the sake of hedging has grown, as has the notional of hedges on the other side of them. Like all things banks, there is a large dispersion in how individual institutions approach this tool in their portfolio man- agement, with just under half of the largest 50 appearing to use PLM at all. The Fed and its monetary policies play the leading role, while fiscal policy and overseas monetary policies play supporting roles. The Fed's interest rate policy, and forward guidance around it, drives rate expectations, and rate expectations have been the largest driver of 10y yields historically. 10y rate expectations moved in a 500 basis point (bp) range prior to the advent of quantitative easing (QE), whereas 10y term premiums moved in a 300bp range. This rebalancing in global demand is at the core of our outlook narrative, which has anticipated a cyclical lift outside tech as last year’s business sentiment shock fades. August survey readings show our business composite expectations index more than reversing this decline and aligning with the pickup in non-tech business spending. Demand rebalancing has not, however, been accompanied by balanced income gains. Global profits surged 35%oya in the second quarter, with MSCI-reported profit growth accelerating in 24 of the 28 tracked economies (Figure 2). In the US, corporate profits jumped 9.1% last quarter (non-annualized) and are up 23%oya. The rising inflation and weak job growth that contributed to this outcome has depressed household real purchasing power across most of the globe. Global CPI inflation is moving lower this quarter — we are tracking a deceleration to 2.5%ar this quarter from last quarter’s 5%ar spike — but the income rebalancing that we anticipate requires firmer labor demand. Budget requests for FY27 are reaching their culmination. Reports indicate that requests in the total general account will exceed ¥130trn. How will this figure translate to the final fiscal size and deficit for the fiscal year? Predicting this will require an accurate understanding of five indicators: budget requests, initial budget, supplementary budget and final settlement, all of which indicate the scale of the budget, and SNA-based expenditures, which serve as a standard for international comparison. It is important first to understand that the summer requests are merely a provisional discussion on the expenditure side. Its figures are highly fluid. Total budget requests include large-scale nondiscretionary items such as national debt servicing, local allocation tax grants, and social security expenses, as well as discretionary policy- based spending at each ministry and agency, which is provisional. The contents will change significantly toward the final compilation of the budget at year-end. With approximately 17 trading days4 remaining between now and the IG roll, and 22 trading days between now and the HY roll, we examine how each index performed over the same respective period for the seventeen rolls since 2017 (excluding 2020). CDX.IG: Historical tightening into the roll Historically, CDX.IG has had a tendency to tighten into the roll, with 2bp of tightening on a median basis across the 17 observed rolls (Figure 5), and spreads tightening in 13 out of 17 rolls (as shown by the "% of obvs wider" series in Figure 5 and in more detail in Figure 6). The main exceptions to this tightening trend all coincided with periods of elevated macro volatility: the regional bank crisis in March 2023, the tariff uncertainty in March 2025, and the Iran conflict in March 2026. CDX.HY: Mixed bag ahead of the HY roll, but a stronger pattern ahead of the IG roll There is less of a discernible pattern for CDX.HY (using a period of 22 business days since HY rolls a week after IG), with spreads tightening into the roll about as often as they have widened (Figure 7 and Figure 8). records.text: M Idea 20 Energy: Sector Analyst View by Martijn Rats, Guilherme Levy & Alice Winograd The situation in the Middle East remains unresolved. As long as this uncertainty persists, we see scope for continued volatility in oil and gas markets and believe the current tightness in supply & demand balances could persist for longer. In our view, the Energy sector offers a degree of protection in an uncertain geopolitical environment, while also providing an attractive hedge against inflation risks. Within the sector, Subsea7 is currently one of our preferred stocks. The company sits in a sweet spot within the Energy Services industry, with exposure to long-cycle oil and gas projects that we expect to proceed despite near-term commodity price volatility. At the same time, demand for offshore services is at its highest level since the early 2010s, while industry capacity has contracted significantly over the same period. This should allow the remaining players to sustain higher margins for longer. We do not believe this favourable backdrop is yet fully reflected in share prices, which continue to trade at depressed levels relative to the period before the 2014 oil price crash. records.text: Global Metals Weekly | 27 August 2026 9 launched a broader review of critical mineral stockpiling. This could mark the beginning of a renewed strategic stockpile policy for tin. The US Defense Logistics Agency historically accumulated substantial refined tin inventories during and after World War II to guard against supply disruptions, with holdings reaching approximately 128kt as recently as 1995 before declining to less than 4kt today. Given rising geopolitical competition and growing concerns over critical mineral security, a return to strategic stockpiling cannot be ruled out. China has also become more proactive in sourcing feedstock China is also placing increasing emphasis on securing long-term tin supply. Although the country is the world’s largest tin smelter and one of the largest consumers of refined tin, domestic processing capacity remains heavily reliant on imported concentrates, particularly from Myanmar, but also from suppliers such as Indonesia and the DRC. Recent disruptions in those countries have highlighted the vulnerability of this model and reinforced the importance of securing upstream resources. Against this backdrop, Chinese companies have increasingly pursued overseas tin investments. Most notably, Inner Mongolia Xingye Silver & Tin acquired a controlling stake in Morocco’s Achmmach project in 2025 before moving to full ownership in 2026. records.text: TenneT Germany (TENNGR): A smart move into the hybrid space Barclays Rating: Market Weight Rating agencies (Moody's/S&P/Fitch): Senior unsecured debt – Baa1 Stab / BBB+ Stab / A- Stab Hybrids rating – Baa2 Stab / NR / BBB Stab After its inaugural €3.5 bn senior issuance in July, TenneT Germany issued its first two green hybrids on 25 August 2026: TENNGR €1.2bn 4.375% 31-56 (NC5.25) and TENNGR €1.4bn 4.75% 34-57 (NC8.5). The structure of TenneT Germany's hybrids is in line with European standards, having 25 and 75bp step-ups in place that trigger the loss of the S&P's 50% equity content at first call date (provided the issuer remains IG). As a result, call and replacement economics at issuer level remain S&P driven, with calling and replacing the hybrids remaining in the issuer's best interest as long as the issuer rating and senior spreads remain in IG territory. As is the case for most of S&P-rated corporate hybrid issuers, extension risk is therefore extremely limited, which results in a compressed senior-sub spread differential and highly efficient hybrid costs from a company perspective. While achieving 50% equity content from all three rating agencies, TenneT Germany did not ask S&P to rate its hybrids. In our view, S&P would likely have rated TenneT Germany's hybrids BB+ (i.e. two notches below the issuer stand-alone rating of 'bbb'), placing them in crossover territory rather than the full IG category assigned by Moody's (Baa2) and Fitch (BBB). CITI'S TAKE Presently there is no confirmation for the start of a structural turning point in global currency policy such as the Plaza Accord of 1985. That said, the recent concerted intervention under the “currency alliance” between the US and Japan could be seen as sign of change in global policy. If the reversal in JPY weakness contributes to a further correction in CNY weakness, the possibility that European nations could participate in the framework and join with the US to demand China reverse CNY depreciation cannot be ruled out. We believe efforts to rectify global imbalances led by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent are likely to adopt an approach completely different from that of the Plaza Accord. Even so, recent JPY weakness, primarily driven by yen-selling hedges linked to the stock market rally, will be difficult to correct. This is likely to be an obstacle to the authorities' attempts. As we show in Figure 24, a $16bn long-risk base, while noting the generally weak relationship, would indicate an actual roll that is perhaps 0.5bp flatter than fair value. • Xover currently has a small short-risk base to roll, in contrast to what prevailed at the prior roll with a short-risk base of $19bn. However, given S44 was a "tranche series" , the large short-risk base did not roll much, and remained in place as hedges against sold protection in tranches. This means the comparison with the prior roll is less relevant, in our view. Instead, as we show in Figure 24, a short-risk base of $2bn, as seen currently, would historically imply a near-flat roll to fair value, with a likely bias to a roll flat to fair value. • CDX.IG and CDX.HY positioning look fairly similar to the previous roll, but we have found very little relationship historically between positioning in these indices and how the roll trades on day 1. Since positioning tends to be long-risk in both indices, the normal expectation is that the traded roll will trade flatter than fair value due to the imbalance of investor long-risk and short-risk positions. For CDX.IG in particular, with the upcoming roll likely to be the steepest since 2021, we think long-risk investors will be incentivized to roll early, which should cause the traded roll to be flatter than fair value. 28 August 2026 21 Barclays | European Credit Alpha: Active tape, earnings and yields provide cover

Aftermarket is a safe haven for many given sustained visible earnings growth, although this comes against the backdrop of normalised air traffic demand, and we generally see less room for upside given elevated expectations and valuations. The exception is Rolls-Royce (Overweight, Top Pick), where we continue to see upside risk driven by the multi-year transformation strategy. In OE, we think the recent introduction of medium-term guidance and a buyback at Airbus (Overweight) represents an important shift in the equity story that is yet to be fully appreciated, and we expect further ramp-up progress in the 12-24 months ahead, supported by further supply chain performance. Rolls Royce (OW, Top Pick) - The Transformation Flywheel Keeps Turning: The turnaround continues to create value ahead of expectations as commercial discipline, operational excellence, and efficient capital allocation align. This is compounded by cost, pricing, and cultural actions as part of the transformation plan. In the ECB’s current framework, this means moving from a “measured” tightening to a “forceful ” tightening. This requires the ECB to believe that the inflation shock is mov ing from a ‘large but not too persistent’ shock to a ‘more significant and sustained overshoot of the target’. There are different routes to believing in a more significant and sustained overshoot of the inflation target. One would be if energy prices remain at elevated levels for longer than expected. Oil prices are in line with baseline, but gas prices are more consistent with the adverse scenario (at least in the near term). Given the lagged transmission of rising gas prices into inflation, this could add persistence to the headline HICP shock, lengthening the period during which energy inflation could spillover into core. records.text: search Banks and other rate-sensitive domestic plays have historically borne the brunt of spread widening, whereas exporters have proved more resilient. We therefore focus on the interaction between spread sensitivity and valuation to identify where France-specific risks are already reflected and where further de-rating remains possible. On that basis, Basic Resources and Transportation look relatively exposed, combining high sensitivity to OAT-Bund spreads with valuation premiums to European peers. By contrast, Banks already trade at a discount, suggesting more of the France risk premium is reflected in prices. Indeed, French Banks have ben hit by recent headlines, with several names down c10% from the early August highs and already trading at a significant discount to other EU banks. With part of the political risk likely priced in already and fundamentals still strong, we would not sell the space now as we rather see potential for a near-term bounce if budget concerns wane. However, we acknowledge that French banks' performance is likely to remain influenced by political noise and may be seen as a bellwether for sentiment on the country. 28 August 2026 6 Barclays | European Equity Strategy

records.text: US Rates Strategy 28 August 2026 Citi Research 3 Last week, we bought 20y bonds as we saw a better risk/reward than in the front-end, which remains exposed to near-term data and uncertainty around Chair Warsh’s reaction function (pricing is 97-22 as of 11:30am on 8/28/26; US Rates Strategy - Getting long 20y after today’s buyback announcement). We continue to like being long the 20y point, which now has the new Treasury “put” on top of our expectation for pension fund demand if 30s retest 5.3%. To be clear, we think a large rally in the 20y is only likely in a world where inflation is normalizing and real money can once again extend out further in the curve, but the point remains protected as any front-end selloff is likely to be a flattener. We do not think 20s will selloff materially if Warsh remains on pause at the September FOMC. Presumably, a pause would be due to another ‘soft’ CPI print, which should not put upward pressure on 30y yields. We also remain received the October FOMC meeting in swaps (pricing of FFX6 is 96.145 as of 11:30am on 8/28/26; US Rates Strategy - FOMC takeaways). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 $4/gallon across much of the US, but diesel prices have returned to April-May highs. Reflecting the slower road to full recovery in oil supply and refinery capacity, our commodity team raised its price target for Brent this week. Previously the team forecasted $75/bbl for Brent through year-end, and that now stands at $90/bbl for 3Q and $100/bbl in 4Q (see Slower Road to Full Recovery; Raising Brent Forecasts). Our "oil risk premium" alternative scenario for the US economy that we highlighted in our mid-year economic update doesn't want to go away just yet. The longer oil prices remain elevated, the greater the risk of elevated headline inflation and second round pass-through into core. We retain our outlook for no hikes this year, but it is a closer call now Although our forecast for inflation has worsened, we maintain our outlook for the Fed to stay on hold this year on account of near-term inflation trends. The July inflation data and revisions imply core PCE inflation running at a 3‑month annualized pace of 3.05% (3.11% in June), a 6‑month pace of 3.46% (3.87% in June), and a 12‑month rate of 3.34% in July (vs. 3.34% in June). Hence, even with upward revisions to prior data, trends still point to lower inflation ahead. In addition, market-based core PCE came in at 0.15% m/m in July, with a 3-month annualized pace of 2.3%. records.text: Barclays Research • We continue to prefer Germany over France. Germany combines improving activity momentum, greater fiscal flexibility and more favourable macro dynamics, even though politics and a rebound in energy prices are risks to monitor. Our German recovery basket (BCERGERE) is lagging improving fundamentals. In contrast, French domestics remain the cleaner expression of sovereign, fiscal and political risk through the cycle. Budget showdown to kick-start a packed agenda for France Presidential race kicks-off amid fragile fiscal position France is entering a busy sequence of fiscal, rating and political events, likely to keep markets on edge into the 2027 presidential election. Both French equities and bonds have come under renewed pressure recently, with the wider OAT-Bund spread translating into underperformance of domestically exposed stocks. Fiscal and political woes are arguably well documented already, but the noise is likely to remain elevated, in our view, keeping investors on the sidelines despite the potential for relief rallies. Although the presidential election in Apr-May 2027 is still a long way away and the race is wide open, polling continues to point to strong support for the political extremes. Marine Le Pen, the far right leader of the RN party, keeps running well ahead in the polls (see Figure 3), followed by the far left leader from the LFI party, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Cash bonds have generally outperformed swaps across the G10, with GDP-weighted EGBs and Gilts being notable exceptions. From a valuation perspective, 10y ACGBs and 10y SGBs appear the cheapest on our twin-deficit framework, while Swiss Confederation bonds and NGBs screen as the richest. On our NIIP mapping, Swiss and US 10y and 30y bonds remain among the richest, while 10y Gilts and 30y JGBs appear the cheapest in their respective sectors. Term premium analysis suggests that Japanese cash and swap 5s10s term premia remain elevated, while Swiss and US term premia appear compressed. Seasonally, term premia tend to decline during the first half of August and rise during the second half of September and first half of October. This year, however, the typical August decline failed to materialise in most markets, with Japan 5s10s swap term premium being the notable exception. While seasonal patterns point to higher term premia into autumn, macro developments are likely to remain the dominant driver. Please click here to read the complete report. With Jackson Hole in the wings, Warsh will need to provide insight into how he intends to deal with Bessent’s attempts to directly influence long yields. Unprecedented: Treasury Secretary Bessent has guided the department into uncharted territory several times over the past quarter. From FX intervention to an attempt at YCC, Treasury is pulling on levers that have rarely been used in recent memory. And while there is a creativity to these attempts, investors have generally faded the initial knee-jerk reaction to these announcements, highlighting the challenges that Treasury ha s in permanently impacting valuations. As ironic as it sounds, Treasury has limited firepower without the Fed, despite (or possibly because of) unprecedented deficit and debt levels. We ultimately think this is a tradable pattern, even as Bessent becomes more outlandish in his attempts to push forward on the Administration’s agenda. This is not to say that there will be no market impact, with the potential for large shifts in both reserves and duration in the coming quarters. We ultimately feel that these efforts will be for naught but will dissect the goals and stress points of Treasury’s current major initiatives. records.text: 7/2/2/24 Source: J.P. Morgan In funding markets, repo has remained contained, with SOFR trading in the range of - 1bp to +1bp to IORB all week. Looking ahead, we expect funding markets to modestly firm from here with month-end coming up, however we expect any firming to be subdued and short-lived; indeed, month-end looks set to be a non-event, with over-the- turn GC repo indications at 3.72%, not dissimilar from the prior few month-ends. Looking further ahead into September, we do not expect any long-lasting pressures in funding as we enter a period of negative T-bill supply next month; we only expect modest firming around the corporate tax date and quarter-end. Against this backdrop, we continue to believe September SOFR/FF (SERFFU6) pricing looks broadly fair at -0.5bp to -1.0bp (see Short-term fixed income). Against this backdrop of contained funding conditions, we continue to like front-end swap spread wideners for carry. In the long end, swap spreads moved wider and TFP declined as media reports indicated a “senior Treasury official” said buybacks could be funded from the TGA. However, we think the reaction was likely overdone, given that the announced additional buybacks remain relatively small. As yields approach 6%, this bias diminishes and a wider range of bonds become credible CTD candidates. • Second, the 2022 to 2023 selloff created unusually wide coupon dispersion within the deliverable basket. USZ6 includes recently issued 20 year bonds with coupons around 5% alongside 30 year bonds issued in 2020 with coupons around 1.5% ( Exhibit 6 ). In our parallel shock analysis, a roughly 50bp selloff shifts the CTD from the 5% May45s to the 1.375% Aug50s, increasing duration risk by approximately 47%. • Third, the switch has moved into a more valuable part of the rates distribution. records.text: Global Macro Strategy - Views and Trade Ideas 27 August 2026 Citi Research 3 Can the Treasury Twist work? Yes but… Organic consolidation would be healthier than financial repression. As we discuss above and further below, there is no obvious UST back-end problem that needs to be solved. So an issuance twist, combined with less hawkish Fed premium (we remain received October FOMC), should be enough to contain back- end yields. We see three main channels towards calmer UST yields (outside of a growth shock), which are not mutually exclusive: 1. Fed Chair Warsh avoiding hikes in 2026 and giving some slight reaction function hints. This removes the risk of another July meeting reaction and should allow UST yields to move lower with the front end. We could get some hints at Jackson Hole, but we expect little, especially with PCE methodology revisions and Task Force conclusions still to come. This could be a slow burn into year end. Negative USD, positive risk. 2. Treasury Secretary Bessent gives fiscal guidance towards no coupon increases. Reduces supply concerns via financial repression. May have to wait until the November 2nd QRA. Negative USD, positive risk. 3. Fiscal consolidation. Politically tricky, this may have to wait until after the November 3rd mid-term elections. Positive USD, mixed on risk. What about other UST concerns? We outline more UST Q&A below. records.text: M Update 2 2Q26 Growth: Broad-Based Strength Canada’s real GDP rebounded 3.3%Q SAAR in 2Q26 after a revised 0.3% increase in 1Q, exceeding the Bank of Canada’s 2.5% forecast in the July MPR. The upside was broad- based. Final domestic demand accelerated to 3.9%Q SAAR, supported by stronger household consumption and a sharp rebound in private investment, while net exports made a large positive contribution as exports surged and imports were nearly flat. Inventories were the principal offset, subtracting 4.9pp from annualized growth as firms moved from inventory accumulation in 1Q to a sizable drawdown in 2Q. Mechanically excluding the inventory drag, GDP growth would have been roughly 8.2%Q SAAR. The details therefore look even stronger than the headline. Unlike 1Q, when large trade and inventory swings obscured weak domestic demand, 2Q strength was visible across consumption, business investment, residential investment and trade. This is partly a reversal of earlier weakness, particularly in housing and exports, but the breadth of the rebound suggests a genuine improvement in underlying momentum as well. Real GDP per capita also increased by roughly 4.1%Q SAAR, helped by a third consecutive quarterly decline in population. Implications for the Bank of Canada In our view, this report should give the Bank of Canada considerably more confidence that downside risks to economic activity have receded. The ISM index continues to point to solid U.S. manufacturing activity, with the series hav- ing reached its strongest level of the current cycle in the sec- ond half of the year. The ISM-weighted composite of the already released July Empire, Philadelphia, Richmond, and Kansas City Fed surveys slipped to 55.7 from 56.1 in July. However, the decline in the flash PMI suggests manufactur- ing growth may be plateauing in August. The weakness in the preliminary PMI manufacturing reading was attributed to fading precautionary demand from firms that had front-loaded orders during the Middle East conflict amid concerns over higher prices and shipping disruptions. This was reflected in declines in stocks and quantities of pur- chases in August, both of which fell close to pre-conflict lev- els. That said, the July ISM press release noted that “the Cus- tomers’ Inventories Index remained in ‘too low’ territory, contracting at a faster rate,” which could limit the risk of a more material downturn in coming months. Concerns about price increases stemming from persistent sup- ply chain challenges and tariff policies were also evident in qualitative comments from the July ISM report. Price indexes remain elevated despite moderating in recent months. Between H1 2025 and the three month s to July 2026, inflation rose by 20pp in energy, 0.25pp in food, 0.8pp in core goods and remained stable in services ex rent/OER, while falling by 1.1pp in rent/OER. Given the large weight of the latter – 43% of the core basket – this decline subtracted ~45bp from y/y core inflation over the period. Private-sector new rent indicators generally continued to weaken until early this year, pointing to further downside risks for the medium -term CPI rent outlook. More recently, however, signs have emerg ed that the rental market is gradually absorbing excess inventory and market specialists have revised their new rent forecasts higher1. To capture contract-level crowding, we employ our FOMO indicator, defined as the average z-score (using an expanding window) of the 3-, 6-, and 12-month Sharpe ratios for each asset, measuring how stretched the near-term Sharpe ratio is relative to its long- term history. We compute FOMO independently for each generic contract (1st through 4th), so the same commodity can exhibit very different readings across the curve. Combining the two, we retain CFTC positioning as the primary asset-selection signal and use cross-contract FOMO purely to choose the optimal expression of the trade along the curve. Importantly, FOMO selection relies only on the cross-contract ranking, not the absolute level, so the chosen contract simply needs the most extreme FOMO among the 1st–4th generics, even if its absolute reading is not directionally aligned. Specifically, at each weekly rebalance, the strategy proceeds in two stages: 1. Asset selection (CFTC positioning): Rank the universe of 20 commodities by their HP_Score and identify the top 30% (most over-owned, candidates for shorting) and bottom 30% (most under-owned, candidates for longing). 2. Contract selection (FOMO): For each selected commodity, compute FOMO across the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th generic contracts and: a. For long candidates (under-owned), pick the contract with the lowest FOMO b. PLM hedging, introduced in early 2022, with mandatory adoption by 2023, represented the greatest step forward in the accounting treatment of prepayable bank assets in years and was a step forward from the last-of-layer method that came out in 2017. Both focus on a closed portfolio of assets (rather than individual securities), but last-of-layer only allowed for a hedge up to the amount of notional expected to still be outstanding at the end of the hedge term. PLM improved on this, along with other clarifications, by allowing for other “layers” with shorter terms to more effectively hedge the larger outstanding of the securities in earlier periods. records.text: 26 August 2026 Germany Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 Structural transformation continues, but is not yet complete The data also indicate that part of the structural transition in key sectors of German industry has been achieved, albeit not yet fully concluded. For example, in the automotive industry, the share of electric cars in total production is rising. Although the sector's former production level is not in sight, the higher demand for e -cars is currently supporting Germany as a manufacturing location, the world's second largest for e -cars after China. The chemical industry is another example: here, the production of energy-intensive products was particularly hard hit by the war in Ukraine (higher gas prices, lower gas supply). This led to painful production adjustments. But here, too, there are positive signals. At the end of July, for example, BASF reported regarding production at its main plant in Ludwigshafen that the "share of highly competitive production units at the site has risen from 78% to 88%" since 2024. As said before , Germany's industrial transformation is by far not yet complete. Adjustments are likely still to come, particularly regarding employment. Furthermore, the economic policy framework must be improved quickly and comprehensively if the fiscal stimulus is to trigger more than just a flash in the pan in the economy. Belgian flash HICP inflation came in at 4.2%yoy in August, up from 3.7%yoy in July, above our expectation of 4.05%yoy. We downgrade our core HICP inflation estimate for Belgium to 3.2%yoy from 3.3%yoy previously, but revise our energy inflation forecast up notably. Taking the French, Spanish, and Belgian national data into account, we now forecast Euro area headline inflation to rise to 3.35%yoy (vs. 3.36%yoy previously) in August, and revise down our Euro area core inflation forecast by 1bp to 2.54%yoy. records.text: ab 28 August 2026 Global Research US Rates Strategy The Bessent put meets a hawkish Fed Over the past two weeks, the yield curve initially bull flattened in response to Treasury Secretary Bessent’s announcement to double the size of long-end buybacks, before bear flattening this week, primarily in response to Fed Chair Warsh’s hawkish comments in Jackson Hole. On net, 2- and 5-year yields rose 17bp and 12bp, respectively, while 30- year yields fell 5bp over the period. Brent oil prices fell 5% to $89/bbl. Notably, Warsh provided a detailed assessment of the economy and struck a hawkish tone, highlighting that this summer’s encouraging inflation readings don’t indicate meaningful improvement in the underlying trend. Additionally, Warsh clearly stated that short-term interest rates are the predominant tool to achieve the dual mandate, said that he “would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive,” and concluded that if the Fed is not “confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” then it has "more work to do.” This is the closest the Chair has come to flagging hikes, effectively lowering the bar for the Committee to deliver a hike in September. In response, the front end repriced sharply, with markets now priced for 14bp of tightening at next month’s meeting and 59bp of cumulative tightening by June, exceeding the local peak reached ahead of the July FOMC meeting. Indeed, reflecting lower prices for the 2025 crop, convenience-store operators have already begun cutting rice-ball prices. These items could face additional downward pressure from autumn, when the impact of new-crop rice prices emerges. In addition, eating-out items such as curry and rice, pork cutlet set meals and tempura rice bowls show a degree of positive correlation with rice prices ( Figure 6). Although restaurant prices are also affected by the cost of ingredients other than rice and by labor costs, lower rice prices could encourage operators to keep prices unchanged or cut some prices. Imported inflation pressure persists The price of crude oil imported by Japan since April remains elevated. records.text: 28 August 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 9 A more consequential step would be to cut long -end auction sizes. In the August QRA, Treasury subtly hinted at this possibility by replacing “future increases” with “future changes” in its coupon guidance. We view large coupon reductions as unlikely against a backdrop of rising deficits, but even a symbolic reduction in the long end would likely have a significant signaling effect and aggressively flatten the curve, at least early on. Other Medium-term, more ambitious measures could include coordinating with the Federal Reserve to improve the economics of holding Treasuries for foreign official institutions. For example, making the FIMA repo facility more attractive (via pricing or relaxed usage caps) while making the foreign repo pool less attractive could incentivize foreign official institutions to maintain or add to their Treasury holdings at the margin. However, the Fed’s repo facilities fall outside Treasury’s authority, which means Treasury has limited ability to affect such changes beyond simply advocating for them. Another ambitious idea would be to leverage Treasury’s position as senior preferred shareholder in Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to influence the housing agencies to expand their mortgage portfolios. We disagree with the notion that the Global Bond Glut is a one-way ticket to higher yields and steeper curves. Instead, our analysis shows that it has increased the frequency of term premia spikes. We show this more clearly in Figure 12 where we calculate the frequency of G10 term premia spikes. In 2021 and 2025, we saw a frequency of term premia spikes that are typically only seen during recessionary bull steepening events. There has been a regime change, but in curve volatility. This is in line with our overall observation that fiscal fears are somewhat episodic. They become the main market driver at certain times, but they also disappear again without the underlying issues been solved.

Combined with JPY depreciation, this means import-driven inflationary pressure is likely to persist through the summer. As a result, we expect the wave of cost pass-through originating from higher crude oil prices to continue spreading to downstream products, including final consumer goods. Rice prices, by contrast, are likely to exert downward pressure. A leading indicator for new-crop rice prices is down about 40% y/y, and our analysis suggests that rice could reduce core-core CPI by around 0.3pp from October onward (see Rice prices set to fall sharply from autumn, weighing on CPI, 26 August). The pass-through from wage growth to inflation also appears to be losing momentum. Taking these factors into account, we expect core-core inflation to recover above 2%, rise temporarily to around 2.5%, and then decline again before stabilizing at around 2% from summer 2027 onward. Monetary policy (last updated 28 August) At the July meeting, the BoJ stepped up its vigilance around the risk that underlying inflation could overshoot above 2%, while also suggesting the possibility of accelerating its previous rate hike pace of roughly once every six months. records.text: et towards the exit. Our investor behavior has shown a clear lack of real money appetite for the long end, particularly from foreign money managers. These challenges along with structural limitations created after decades of profligate government spending is largely behind our skepticism around any long lasting impact in demand for duration. In fact, we think Bessent’s interventionist efforts may do more harm than good. We see his recent attempts as putting a spotlight on debt (un)sustainability, which all investors know well and good, even if there is a dearth of alternative safe assets globally. More troubling is that he may force the Fed to take a more aggressive stance in the treasury market to either counterbalance looser financial conditions or ensure financial stability as treasury issuance becomes more unbalanced. Relying on the short e nd works well in an abundant liquidity regime but becomes more complicated with scarce reserves and bills closer to 30% of outstanding (presently at 22%, up from 14% before Covid). While this may eventually require an implicit Fed/Treasury agreement, investors would likely see through the folly and further punish the long end as policy credibility is called into question. We therefore remain structurally underweight duration as the Gordian Knot tightens. Subsequent work advanced this framework beyond a simple linear combination of instrument-level skewness by distinguishing two profit drivers, market skewness and residual skewness, and building strategies that optimize each component separately as well as an optimal way to combine them based on their respective profit potential. We found that market skewness primarily drives the signal’s efficacy for most asset classes, while residual skewness dominates in commodities, and we have extended this portfolio-level shaping approach to off-benchmark commodities, single stocks, and generic equity factors. In this publication, we adopt a complementary perspective by constructing a skewness signal grounded in statistical hypothesis testing at the asset level. Rather than optimizing portfolio skewness ex ante, we test for each asset at each point in time whether its return distribution exhibits statistically significant skewness, translating the strength of that evidence into a bounded trading signal. records.text: Higher Product Margins for Longer on Higher Outages and Lower Stocks Back in February, we argued that tight global refining capacity, following years of insufficient refinery additions, would keep margins higher for longer. Rising strikes on refineries in the Middle East and Russia have further constrained already-stretched global refining capacity, pushing refined product margins to new highs to incentivize refiners to run harder. The average wholesale price of global refined products doubled during the first two months of the US-Iran war and, even after some moderation in June, is still up nearly $50 year-over-year (yoy) (Exhibit 1, left panel). Diesel remains at the epicenter of the rally, accounting for over 40% of the $40/bbl increase in average global refined product prices since the end of February (Exhibit 1, right panel). While prospects for a recovery in Middle Eastern and especially Russian refinery runs are unclear and crude deliveries to Asia remain disrupted, refined product stocks continue to draw. We upgrade our diesel and gasoline margins forecast for the US, Europe and Asia, and now expect US/Europe diesel margins vs. Brent to average $63/49/bbl in 2027 (vs. $27/19 in February), slightly above market forwards (Exhibit 2). records.text: M Idea 2 Prices up, costs flat, profits soar The 2Q profit surge looks more like margin expansion than a nominal GDP story Corporate profits of the non-financial corporate sector were up a startling $400.9bn in 2Q 2026 (q/q saar), resulting in one of the largest (non-post recession) quarterly improvements in recent decades ( Exhibit 2 ). At 15.2%, the profit margin for the non- financial corporate sector, defined as profits as a share of gross value added, remains near all-time highs in the post-war period ( Exhibit 3 ). What's going on and can this continue? One possible explanation is that strong nominal growth is boosting corporate profitability. There is some truth to the conventional wisdom that a high nominal growth environment is good for corporate profits since nominal GDP is a useful reduced-form indicator of the nominal revenue environment facing corporations. A positive relationship between nominal GDP and nominal corporate profits should be expected – GDP and GDI are two measures of the same economic activity – and corporate profits are themselves a component of national income. Moreover, inflation can raise the nominal scale of both GDP and profits. If all prices, wages and other nominal costs doubled while quantities and relative prices were unchanged, nominal GDP and nominal profits would approximately double. Exhibit 2: The $400.9bn increase in corporate profits in 2Q 26 was the largest quarterly percentage increase since 2010 (outside the pandemic). -200 -100

records.text: ort should give the Bank of Canada considerably more confidence that downside risks to economic activity have receded. The 3.3%Q SAAR headline exceeded the Bank’s 2.5% July forecast, but the more important surprise was the composition. Household consumption grew considerably faster than the Bank expected, private investment rebounded sharply, and final domestic demand rose 3.9%. The Bank had explicitly been looking for evidence that the recovery was broadening, and this report provides a fairly clean signal that it is. The report also looks consistent with the recent improvement in labor-market data: activity is no longer being supported solely by one or two volatile expenditure categories. That said, we do not think stronger growth by itself creates a compelling case for a rate hike. In the July MPR, the BoC continued to characterize inflation excluding gasoline and core inflation as close to 2%, even as headline inflation was temporarily elevated by energy prices. Our assessment of recent data is similar. In our view, this report reduces the probability of renewed easing rather than increase the probability of tightening, given a limited pass-through to core inflation. We continue to expect the BoC to remain on hold through 2026.

Investments are still lackluster, a clear sign that not all is well with the European business cycle. As we went through the data received over the summer in our weekly last Friday (here), one of the most intriguing prints was the strength of EA growth in 2Q26. It stood at a quarterly pace of 0.44%Q or 1.8% annualized (higher than in the US in that quarter). While the detailed GDP components for the EA will be published only on 7 September by Eurostat, we know already quite a lot from country national accounts (eg Germany, France, Spain and Netherlands – Italy is due on 1 September) and monthly data. To start with the obvious, 2Q was a solid quarter across all European countries. Yet, contrary to other regions in the world, behind the growth strength is not a capex cycle broadening out. Next to solid consumption growth, it is also driven by some factors that are likely temporary (exports of chemical products, for example). Let’s look further into the details. We start with the GDP figures. Excluding Ireland, EA growth stood at 0.3%Q in 2Q26, a broadly unchanged pace since the start of 2025. What is interesting here is that, and contrary to 2025, the aggregate of the four largest economies (Germany, France, Italy and Spain) is not lagging the rest of the region. As we noted in our prior writings, corporate sector behavior in 2026 is similar to COVID. At the time, both labor and nonlabor costs were rising, but the corporate sector increased prices by more than costs rose, raising profitability and margins in the process. At present, firms have responded to higher nonlabor costs by holding back the wage bill and pushing price. The effect of this behavior is producing similar trends in the macro data. Then, as now, inflation reduced purchasing power by putting downward pressure on real income growth and households responded by pushing the saving rate lower. We use a vol-adjusted moving-average crossover overlay across Investment Styles to determine which are reliably trendable, and where timing adds genuine alpha. records.text: 32 Dobromir Tzotchev, PhD AC (44-20) 7134-5331 dobromir.tzotchev@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 28 August 2026 J P M O R G A N Trade Timing: Ten Years On A decade ago we published Trade Timing in Global Equities: Fast-burn signals to enhance slower strategies. The main motivation was that many of the strongest signals in quant (short-term reversion, recommendation changes, RSI) are too expensive to own, because their turnover destroys the alpha at any realistic transaction cost. So rather than compromise the net power of a cross-sectional composite, we proposed using them as trade-timing overlays: keep buying what the slow strategy wants, but only when a faster signal agrees. The back-tests of the time showed higher performance on lower turnover across all MSCI regions, and the framework has since been adopted as part of our regular quant work. Ten years on, we revisit the study in Ten Years On... Revisiting Fast-Burning Signals for Slower Quant Strategies in Global Equities. The post- publication period (June 2016 to date) is now a clean out-of-sample window, and it has been an unusually punishing one for factor investors. If trade timing was a regime- conditional artifact of the 1995–2016 sample, then it might have struggled since. But the framework still holds up. Trade Timing is a simple idea: combine a slow strategy with a fast timing signal, and let the fast signal decide when the slow can act. Page 5 JGB: This Week in Review, The Week Ahead JGB Implications of the FY2027 Budget Requests Budget requests should be regarded as establishing a floor for the eventual fiscal envelope rather than a ceiling. Media reports indicate that FY2027 general-account requests will exceed JPY130tn, marking a record high for a fourth consecutive year, while our economists employ a working assumption of approximately JPY135tn. In light of unspecified requests, uncapped investment allocations and the policy shift towards incorporating recurring measures in the initial budget, however, this figure should be viewed only as a conservative starting point for the year-end budget process. Indeed, JPY135tn would already exceed the final FY2025 budget after supplementary appropriations, which amounted to JPY133.5tn. The revenue outlook presents a still more significant challenge. The proposed reduction in the consumption-tax rate on food from 8% to 1% from April 2027 would lower annual revenue by approximately JPY5.8tn. Taken together, upside risks to expenditure and downside risks to revenue support our base-case expectation that new JGB issuance will rise from the FY2026 initial level of JPY29.6tn into the JPY30tn range. This would not, however, necessarily entail an increase in super-long issuance. The MoF has reduced super-long supply for two consecutive years and lowered calendar-based market issuance to JPY168.5tn

Mythbusting reasons for higher UST yields Reason #1: UST yields have a fiscal problem Keeping it real – yields are here due to energy and growth. Breaking down the move in the 30y UST into component parts sheds light on the story (Figure 3). We decompose the 30y UST into 30Y SOFR real yield, plus 30y inflation swap, plus the inverse of the 30y ASW (UST – SOFR yield in this instance) as a barometer of fiscal risk premium. As we can see, the bulk of the YTD move, and especially since July, has been led by the real yield. The inflation breakeven rally has been mild, and if anything, fiscal risk premia has compressed recently. The move in yields has mostly correlated with cyclical moves in energy prices and equities (Figure 4). This signals three things to us: 1) Fiscal does not seem to be the main concern, given that ASW did not reflect fiscal fears; 2) there are only limited structural inflation concerns embedded in UST yields, mostly limited to Iran risk; 3) We note that positive growth dynamics driven by the US AI expansion are potentially raising R*, which is a better explanation of what has been driving rates. Figure 5 shows two measures of productivity rising with 5y5y real yields. Profit margins, which were already high post-COVID, advanced again to historically elevated levels. Our FAB index dropped midweek after a sharp move lower in USD yields post the Treasury’s buyback announcement, but yields have since reversed completely such that the index moved back up. The Forward FAB index is 8bp higher than the FAB index currently, implying modest upside for the index. USD IG Corps are screening more attractive versus EUR corporates for most currencies at both the 10y and the 30y point. APAC: For JPY investors, the yield give improved by 5bp to -15bp at the 10yr point while it worsened at the 30yr point by 3bp WoW to -77bp, coming off the highs since April 2025 seen last week. For TWD investors, the yield pickup at the 10yr point fell by 4bp WoW to 163bp. For AUD investors, the yield pickup at the 10y point also fell modestly by 1bp WoW to +118bp. Americas: For CAD investors, the yield pickup fell 7bp WoW to 20bp

This is more so in the last several years as globalization and broader economic convergence trends between developed economies have rendered geographical boundaries a more faint economic performance differentiator than than they had been in prior years. A pragmatic conclusion here is that one is usually better off not region-picking actively. The message strengthens once costs are accounted for. If, however, the signal is relatively3 strong and, perhaps additionally, if the regional allocation is, in effect, free or cheap (for example a corollary of other concurrent informed investment decisions) then region picking may be worth it in the long run. Region Factor Mimicking Portfolios We need to define pure regions. Much as is the case for pure sectors, pure regions are also rooted in the same idea as pure factors and are built in the same way. So, pure region-factor mimicking portfolios are portfolios that have an exposure of 1 to the targeted region while having no exposure to other regions, sectors or factors. In the context of regions, exposure is based on (equally weighted) membership, albeit adjusted to deal with multicollinearity and thus differing from simple membership dummies of 1s and 0s4. records.text: s the richer risk-off wing of the smile and buys the cheaper risk-on wing. Once delta hedged, the position carries negative vanna. Vanna measures how option delta changes with volatility, or equivalently how vega changes with the underlying spread. Selling the payer and buying the receiver produces the same short-vanna direction on both legs. The trade earns carry when the spread-vol covariance priced into payer skew exceeds the covariance subsequently realised, but loses when spreads and volatility rise together more aggressively than expected. The analogy with conventional volatility carry is useful. Schematically: Variance Trade: Gamma P&L ~ |Gamma| x [Implied Variance - Realised Variance] Skew Trade: Vanna P&L ~ |Vanna| x [Implied Covar(∆S,∆σ) - Realised Covar(∆S,∆σ)] The risk reversal notionals can be selected to reduce exposures that are not central to the skew view. In particular, gamma-neutral sizing removes much of the realised-spread- variance exposure and leaves a cleaner combination of positive theta and negative vanna. While G10 currencies may benefit from fiscal loosening via growth boosts and lower front - end yields, high fiscal vulnerability in EM typically leads to currency weakness, even when local risk premiums are already elevated (Figure 7) To better hedge against US-centric 'fiscal risk-off' events, we have replaced generic FX-fiscal sensitivity measures with a conditional scenario framework. This approach evaluates how FX responds to rising US term premiums and yield curve steepening in particular, while accounting for the local fiscal risk premiums already priced into the majority of the analyzed countries. We isolate days over the past four years where we observe: (1) an increase in the US term premium or a Treasury curve steepening of more than one z-score, and (2) an average z-score for the local term premium and asset-swap spread exceeding 1. July money and credit data Bank lending flows remain robust and continue to support domestic economic activity. Our standard credit impulse—the key downstream cyclical indicator for private domestic demand growth—has demonstrated notable resilience this year, despite the negative signals emerging from the Q2 Bank Lending Survey. July bank lending data was no exception. Although net lending flows to the real economy experienced a minor deceleration in July, the credit impulse edged slightly higher to 1.4pp up from 1.2pp in June, owing to favourable base effects. This moderation in credit flows was primarily driven by a contraction in long-term lending to enterprises, which was only partially offset by a modest recovery in medium-term credit. Because the previous strength in long-term lending had pointed towards the potential initiation of a capital expenditure cycle, these flows will require close monitoring to determine whether the July dip is merely statistical noise or indicative of a more systemic slowdown. Beyond these lending dynamics, the household sector exhibited a notable increase in term deposit flows during July. While US GDP is projected to rise at a 2.75%ar this quarter, we antici- pate a meager 50k job increase next week. Absent revisions, the monthly average gain would slip to 16k for the three months through August. These developments set up a critical test ahead: will the rebal- ancing in demand underway boost job growth, or is structural change related to new technologies and weak labor supply producing a sustained shift towards productivity-led growth? We continue to project a balance between cyclical lift and structural change and expect global job growth to rise to a 1%ar pace, with US gains returning to triple-digits. While recognizing recent disappointments, our confidence that a labor market recoupling remains reasonable is sustained by two recent developments: • A chain from profits to job growth. The recent profit surge has come on the back of weak job growth, but it should also become a catalyst for a rebound. The juxtapo- sition of weak US job growth, strong profits and support- ive credit conditions is not a new one.

Consequently, historically elevated fiscal-risk premiums priced into G10 curves imply that G10 currencies will be more sensitive to US fiscal deterioration than historical patterns would suggest. Drawing on our findings regarding fiscal vulnerability and FX sensitivity, we have constructed a carry- neutral currency basket. To prevent idiosyncratic risks from dominating the portfolio, we utilize risk- weighted allocations based on beta to SPX. The basket is composed of the following weights (aggregated across all cross-pairs): long side: 14% CHF, 49% MYR, 23% CZK, and 14% NOK; short side: 13% USD, 32% PLN, 35% JPY, and 19% MXN. The basket carries a net annualized carry of −0.6% (implied by 12m forwards) and has delivered a year-to-date return of +1.5% (excluding carry, see Figure 6 in Appendix). records.text: European High Yield & Leveraged Loans Picking where the pick-up pays Loans have outperformed bonds, but ratings explain most of the pick-up and the rating momentum is weaker. BB loans have a better outlook, but are a small share and offer limited value vs history. With pending supply set to test valuations, we favour issuer-level switches over a broad preference. Loans have delivered a 2.5% total return year-to-date, outperforming the 2.0% return from bonds despite their greater exposure to the tech-led sell-off earlier in the year. The relative- value case remains supported by a 135bp forward curve-adjusted yield pick-up over bonds, which still ranks at the 77th percentile over the past five years (Figure 1). However, this pick-up reflects the increasingly different rating composition of the two markets. Single Bs account for 82% of the loan index, compared with 32% of the bond index, while BBs represent just 10% of loans versus 62% of bonds. This divergence has widened in recent years: the average rating score of the loan market has deteriorated, while that of the bond market is largely unchanged (Figure 2), although this recent shift does not explain the headline differential. Once we control for the overall ratings mix, the loan yield pick-up falls from 135bp to just over 30bp. On a rating-matched basis, BB loans offer around 90bp over BB bonds, at only the 25th percentile of the past five years, while single-B loans offer a modest 22bp pick-up. The question is therefore

The level and volatility of 30y rates in all major markets have led to various policy responses over the last year, including meaningful reductions of the weighted average maturity (WAM) of issuance in certain markets. The US Treasury’s announcement of increased long-end buybacks is the latest measure. Adjusting issuance on the curve is a natural supply response to shifting patterns of demand, especially the structural reduction in long-end demand from liability-driven investors. However, we see little evidence that these issuance responses can meaningfully impact the broader level of yields—even at the long-end. Over the last year, the UK DMO and Japanese MoF have reduced WAM at issuance via sharp reductions in long-end supply (Exhibit 2). This has had some local success in richening long-end bonds vs swaps, but has not managed to lower the overall level of yields. We think this will be true of issuance-based strategies—their impact is more micro than macro, with only a shift in macro fundamentals towards lower inflation a reliable path to durable relief. 3. The initial budget, determined once spending and revenues are set, serves as the basic plan for the fiscal year. In recent years, however, it has become common practice in Japan to compile supplementary budgets midyear to pay for economic stimulus measures. Therefore, the key figure for understanding the true scale of public finance is the budget after the release of supplementary budgets. The settlement of accounts (the actual figures recorded after the end of the fiscal year) is usually lower than the budget amount including supplementary budgets due to factors such as unspent funds. SNA-based expenditures serve as the international standard for analyzing the macroeconomic impact of these domestic budget indicators. “Central government” under the SNA framework is a concept that consolidates and adjusts the General Account as well as multiple Special Accounts. The resulting expenditure is often lower than the settlement figure in the General Account. For one thing, SNA treats fund transfers (such as inward transfers) between the General and Special Accounts as offsetting internal transactions. More crucially, dept redemption costs, included in General Account expenditures, are classified as financial transactions that generate no added value and are thus excluded from the final SNA figures. records.text: M Idea 14 Higher deficits generally require greater Treasury issuance. All else equal, more Treasury supply should cheapen cash Treasuries relative to swaps, and tighten swap spreads. The historical relationship between the amount of Treasury duration held outside SOMA and 10y swap spreads shows that effect – but also its limits (see Exhibit 30 ). Even where Treasury supply should matter most directly – in the relative price of Treasuries versus swaps – the relationship is not mechanical. A near-record amount of nominal Treasury DV01 sits in private sector hands, yet 10y swap spreads have widened more than 15bp since QT2 ended in December 2025. Since US public debt surpassed $31tr in October 2022, the subsequent $9tr increase coincided with only 13bp of tightening in 10y swap spreads but 4bp of widening in 30y spreads (see Exhibit 31 ). The stock of debt rose; its relative price did not move uniformly. Even where Treasury supply should appear most directly, Fed balance-sheet policy, regulation, investor demand, financing conditions and dealer intermediation capacity also influence the price at which Treasuries clear. That distinction brings us back to who buys the debt? Knowing the identity of the largest holders tells us little about the price established by the marginal buyer or seller. By contrast, if reserve managers reduced their G4 government debt holdings in favour of other asset classes, private investors would need to absorb the debt securities sold by foreign official institutions, increasin g private sector ownership. Given the relatively short maturity profile of these holdings, the WAM of private sector holdings would decline modestly. Overall, the analysis suggests that tracking only the private sector's share of government debt ownership may not be sufficient. The maturity distribution of those holdings also matters. Changes in DMO issuance and buyback strategies, central bank balance sheets and reserve manager allocations can alter not only how much government debt is owned by private investors, but also where along the curve that exposure sits. While we treat the private sector as a single investor group in this analysis, we acknowledge that some investors, such as pension funds and insurance companies, are considerably less price -sensitive than other market participants. Future work will therefore seek to further decompose private sector holdings by investor type and maturity bucket. For HY, with yields at 5.9% and a duration of 3.1, the equivalent monthly break-even increase is 16bp. As such, as long as IG yields do not rise by more than 7bp per month, or 16bp for HY, total returns will remain positive and, in turn, retail flows are unlikely to become a headwind. European Equity Strategy France – Deficits, elections and déjà vu French bonds and equities have come under renewed pressure amid concerns about a budget showdown and the 2027 presidential election. Risk premium is arguably high already, but fiscal concerns and political uncertainty are likely to persist, weighing on French domestics (BCERFRSK). We prefer Germany. • France is entering an extended period of fiscal and political uncertainty, with budget negotiations, rating reviews and the 2027 presidential election race likely to keep investors on edge. Polls have the far right leader Marine Le Pen in the lead, followed by the far left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon. For now, with deficits expected to remain above 5% of GDP , debt topping 120% of GDP and growth still subdued, meaningful consolidation looks unlikely, supporting a structurally wider spread regime vs. EU peers.

records.text: M Idea 2 Upward revisions to core PCE inflation means the Fed has less margin for error First, the good news: July inflation points to disinflation July PCE inflation data came broadly in line with expectations, with headline and core PCE inflation rising by a fairly muted 0.2% m/m, for annual increases of 3.7% at the headline and 3.3% at the core. Core goods rose in July on account of AI-related inflation for computers, peripherals, and smart home assistants, likely reflecting Apple price increases implemented in late June. That said, our models continue to suggest that we are at, or very close to, the finish line for tariff pass-through. We estimate that tariffs have added roughly 60bp to PCE prices so far, and the recently announced Section 338 tariffs on Canadian exports do not materially alter our outlook (they raise the overall effective U.S. tariff rate by only 0.2pp). Hence, significant tariff pass through remains in the pipeline. On net, we read the July PCE inflation data as consistent with our outlook for slowing inflation. Now the bad news: Upward revisions to core inflation Core inflation in 2Q was revised higher The bad news came in the area of core PCE inflation, where the quarterly annualized pace was revised higher by two-tenths to 3.6%. The upward revisions were largely explained by non-profit institutions serving households. Our 4Q/4Q forecast for core PCE inflation is now 3.2% for 2026. records.text: 9 Dobromir Tzotchev, PhD AC (44-20) 7134-5331 dobromir.tzotchev@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 28 August 2026 J P M O R G A N premia. In Profiting from the third moment in GEFs, we extend our skewness strategy to GEFs focusing on the market, the residual and the optimal skewness approaches. In this publication, we use the skewness as a timing signal for cross-asset risk premia strategies. For each strategy, we compute the skewness over five lookback windows of 65, 130, 260, 520 and 1300 days and take the average across them as the final skew signal. As with spillover momentum, we begin by comparing unoptimized baseline performance at the strategy level. Since the objective is to be long assets with negative skew, at each month-end we go long when the skew signal is negative; otherwise, we exit the position. Positions are sized proportionally to the magnitude of negative skew (i.e., −skew when skew <0) and inversely to asset volatility. Then we target 7% annualized volatility on expanding window.
